s23e-s08b02.bodyHtml:
Chemical injury: irrigate first

  1. Start copious irrigation at once, before taking a history, measuring visual acuity or examining. Tap water is acceptable at the scene; in hospital use normal saline or lactated Ringer solution, with a topical anaesthetic drop and a lid speculum or irrigating lens to keep the eye open.
  2. Sweep the fornices for retained particles (lime, cement).
  3. Check the tear-film pH with a strip a few minutes after stopping. Continue until it is neutral (about 7.0–7.5).
  4. Then examine (acuity, fluorescein, pressure) and refer urgently to ophthalmology.

Corneal abrasion

  • Fluorescein examination; evert the upper lid to look for a foreign body.
  • Topical antibiotic: erythromycin ointment or a similar agent; for contact lens wearers, an anti-pseudomonal fluoroquinolone drop, no lens wear until healed, and no patching.
  • Oral analgesia or topical NSAID. Never send the patient home with a topical anaesthetic.
  • Re-examine in 24–48 hours if large, central or in a lens wearer.

Corneal foreign body: remove a superficial one under topical anaesthesia with a needle or burr at the slit lamp. A high-velocity injury (hammering metal on metal, grinding) can drive a particle into the globe: get CT of the orbits and avoid MRI until a metallic foreign body is excluded.

Open globe

  • Place a rigid shield that rests on the bony orbit; no pressure on the eye, no pressure measurement, no topical drops or ointment.
  • Keep the patient nil by mouth, give analgesia and an antiemetic (vomiting and straining raise eye pressure), update tetanus and start systemic antibiotics against endophthalmitis.
  • CT of the orbits; emergency ophthalmology for surgical repair. Do not remove a protruding object.

Hyphema

  • Rigid shield, head of the bed raised about 30–45°, rest, and avoidance of NSAIDs and antiplatelet drugs.
  • Ophthalmology manages topical steroid and cycloplegic drops and checks pressure; rebleeding is most likely in the first days.
  • Screen patients at risk (for example, of African ancestry) for sickle cell disease or trait; in these patients, avoid carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and osmotic agents, which can promote sickling or hypovolaemia.

Orbital floor fracture

  • CT of the orbits with thin cuts. Advise no nose blowing.
  • Urgent surgery for entrapment with an oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia, nausea, syncope) — classic in children, whose flexible floor can snap back and trap the muscle while the eye looks only mildly injured.
  • Otherwise repair is often elective, within about 2 weeks, for persistent diplopia, large defects or enophthalmos.

Retrobulbar haemorrhage

Proptosis, a tense orbit, falling vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect and high intraocular pressure after trauma (or orbital or sinus surgery) need lateral canthotomy with inferior cantholysis at the bedside. It is a clinical diagnosis; do not delay decompression for imaging.

Exam trap: the first step for a chemical splash is irrigation, even before visual acuity. For an open globe it is a shield, and nothing that presses on the eye or enters it.

s23e-s08b03.bodyHtml:
Monitoring that prevents permanent loss

DrugWhat to do
HydroxychloroquineKeep the daily dose at or below 5 mg/kg of actual body weight. Baseline examination early in treatment, then yearly screening from 5 years of use (sooner with renal impairment, tamoxifen use, higher doses or macular disease), with optical coherence tomography and automated visual fields. Toxicity is irreversible and can progress after stopping, so the aim is to stop before symptoms.
EthambutolBaseline acuity and colour vision; ask about vision at every visit and retest regularly, more often with renal impairment or higher doses. Stop the drug at the first sign of toxicity and refer.
VigabatrinBaseline and periodic visual field testing; field loss is permanent.
FingolimodFundus examination including the macula before starting and again 3–4 months after, and at any visual change; diabetes and uveitis raise the risk of macular oedema.
Long-term glucocorticoidsPeriodic eye pressure checks and cataract surveillance, especially with steroid eye drops.

Drug-triggered acute angle closure

  • Pupillary-block type (antimuscarinics, adrenergic mydriatics in a narrow-angle eye): a painful red eye, blurred vision with haloes, headache and vomiting, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and a hazy cornea. Lower the pressure at once (topical beta-blocker, alpha-2 agonist and miotic drops, systemic acetazolamide or mannitol), then laser peripheral iridotomy in both eyes.
  • Topiramate type (bilateral, myopic shift, first weeks of treatment): stop topiramate, use aqueous suppressants and cycloplegic drops to deepen the chamber; avoid pilocarpine and iridotomy, which do not work and may worsen it.

Other effects to recognise

  • Tamsulosin: tell the cataract surgeon before surgery; stopping it beforehand does not reliably prevent floppy iris.
  • Amiodarone: corneal deposits need no action. New visual loss with disc swelling raises optic neuropathy: involve cardiology before stopping the drug.
  • Sildenafil: blue-tinged vision is dose-related and reversible. Sudden painless visual loss needs urgent review for ischaemic optic neuropathy.
  • Digoxin: coloured vision suggests toxicity; check the level, potassium, magnesium and renal function.
  • Bisphosphonates: a painful red eye after an infusion may be uveitis or scleritis and needs ophthalmology review.
  • Topical anaesthetic misuse: a non-healing epithelial defect or ring infiltrate in a patient who has been using "numbing drops" at home; stop them and refer.
  • Eye drops with systemic effects: consider timolol in a patient with new bradycardia or wheeze; teach punctal occlusion (pressing the inner corner of the eye after each drop) to reduce absorption.
Exam trap: a patient with a known narrow angle who needs an anticholinergic drug can usually receive it safely after laser iridotomy. Open-angle glaucoma is not a contraindication to anticholinergics.

s23e-s09a01.bodyHtml:
The middle ear is an air-filled space ventilated through the eustachian (auditory) tube, which runs from the anterior wall of the middle ear to the lateral nasopharynx. The tube opens during swallowing and yawning, mainly through contraction of the tensor veli palatini. In young children the tube is shorter, more horizontal and less rigid, so it drains poorly and lets nasopharyngeal secretions reach the middle ear. This is why middle-ear infection peaks between 6 and 24 months of age, often right after a viral upper respiratory infection.

Acute otitis media (AOM)

A viral infection inflames the tube mucosa. The tube then blocks, air in the middle ear is absorbed, negative pressure draws in fluid, and bacteria from the nasopharynx multiply in that fluid. The usual bacteria are:

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae: reduced penicillin susceptibility comes from altered penicillin-binding proteins. Higher amoxicillin doses overcome it, while a beta-lactamase inhibitor does not help against this mechanism.
  • Nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae (unencapsulated, so the Hib vaccine does not prevent it): often produces beta-lactamase. It is the typical cause when otitis comes with purulent conjunctivitis.
  • Moraxella catarrhalis: a gram-negative diplococcus; nearly all strains produce beta-lactamase.

On otoscopy, a bulging tympanic membrane is the most specific sign. Redness alone is not, because crying also reddens the drum. Otitis media with effusion (OME) is fluid without acute inflammation. It commonly follows AOM and causes a mild conductive hearing loss.

Otitis externa

Cerumen keeps the external canal acidic and water-repellent. Repeated wetting (swimming), scratching and cotton swabs strip it, so the skin macerates and becomes infected. Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus cause most cases. The hallmark is pain when the tragus is pressed or the pinna is pulled, because the inflamed canal skin is moved.

Necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa is an invasive Pseudomonas infection, usually in older people with diabetes or other immune compromise. It spreads from the canal floor at the bony-cartilaginous junction into the temporal bone and skull base. Granulation tissue in the canal, pain out of proportion to the findings and facial nerve palsy are warning signs.

Mastoiditis and intracranial spread

The mastoid air cells connect with the middle ear, so AOM can spread into them and erode their bony walls. Pus can track outwards (a postauricular abscess that pushes the auricle forwards and down) or inwards. Inward spread can cause thrombosis of the sigmoid sinus, which lies directly behind the mastoid, as well as meningitis, epidural or brain abscess, and facial nerve palsy.

Cholesteatoma

A cholesteatoma is not a tumour and contains no cholesterol. It is a sac of keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium that keeps shedding keratin into the middle ear or mastoid. Most are acquired, from a retraction pocket of the pars flaccida in a poorly ventilated ear. The sac grows and releases enzymes that erode bone: the ossicles (conductive loss), the lateral semicircular canal (a fistula with vertigo), the facial canal and the tegmen (intracranial infection). The typical clue is painless, foul-smelling discharge that keeps coming back, with white debris on otoscopy.

LesionWhat it is made of
CholesteatomaKeratinizing squamous epithelium and keratin debris
Cholesterol granulomaCholesterol crystals surrounded by foreign-body giant cells and old blood
Granulation tissue (chronic otitis)Capillaries, fibroblasts and inflammatory cells

Herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome)

Varicella-zoster virus reactivates in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve. The result is severe ear pain, vesicles on the concha, canal or palate, and a lower motor neuron facial palsy. The virus can spread to the nearby vestibulocochlear nerve and cause hearing loss and vertigo. Recovery of facial function is worse than in Bell palsy.

Exam trap: "cholesteatoma" and "cholesterol granuloma" sound alike but differ. The first is skin (keratin) in the wrong place, the second a reaction to old blood.
Pearl: an older person with diabetes, severe ear pain and granulation tissue on the canal floor has an invasive Pseudomonas infection of the skull base until proven otherwise.

, which runs from the anterior wall of the middle ear to the lateral nasopharynx. The tube opens during swallowing and yawning, mainly through contraction of the tensor veli palatini. In young children the tube is shorter, more horizontal and less rigid, so it drains poorly and lets nasopharyngeal secretions reach the middle ear. This is why middle-ear infection peaks between 6 and 24 months of age, often right after a viral upper respiratory infection.

A viral infection inflames the tube mucosa. The tube then blocks, air in the middle ear is absorbed, negative pressure draws in fluid, and bacteria from the nasopharynx multiply in that fluid. The usual bacteria are:
. Higher amoxicillin doses overcome it, while a beta-lactamase inhibitor does not help against this mechanism.
(unencapsulated, so the Hib vaccine does not prevent it): often produces beta-lactamase. It is the typical cause when otitis comes with purulent conjunctivitis.
: a gram-negative diplococcus; nearly all strains produce beta-lactamase.

tympanic membrane is the most specific sign. Redness alone is not, because crying also reddens the drum. Otitis media with effusion (OME) is fluid without acute inflammation. It commonly follows AOM and causes a mild conductive hearing loss.
Cerumen keeps the external canal acidic and water-repellent. Repeated wetting (swimming), scratching and cotton swabs strip it, so the skin macerates and becomes infected.
cause most cases. The hallmark is pain when the tragus is pressed or the pinna is pulled, because the inflamed canal skin is moved.

The mastoid air cells connect with the middle ear, so AOM can spread into them and erode their bony walls. Pus can track outwards (a postauricular abscess that pushes the auricle forwards and down) or inwards. Inward spread can cause thrombosis of the
, which lies directly behind the mastoid, as well as meningitis, epidural or brain abscess, and facial nerve palsy.
A cholesteatoma is not a tumour and contains no cholesterol. It is a sac of

that keeps shedding keratin into the middle ear or mastoid. Most are acquired, from a retraction pocket of the pars flaccida in a poorly ventilated ear. The sac grows and releases enzymes that erode bone: the ossicles (conductive loss), the lateral semicircular canal (a fistula with vertigo), the facial canal and the tegmen (intracranial infection). The typical clue is painless, foul-smelling discharge that keeps coming back, with white debris on otoscopy.

"cholesteatoma" and "cholesterol granuloma" sound alike but differ. The first is skin (keratin) in the wrong place, the second a reaction to old blood.

s23e-s09a02.bodyHtml:
Vestibular schwannoma

A benign tumour of Schwann cells, usually arising from the vestibular division of cranial nerve VIII inside the internal auditory canal. It grows slowly and extends into the cerebellopontine angle. Histology shows cellular areas with nuclear palisading around pink fibrillar zones (Antoni A, with Verocay bodies) next to loose, myxoid areas (Antoni B). The cells are S-100 positive.

  • Early: slowly progressive one-sided sensorineural hearing loss, often with tinnitus. Imbalance is usually mild because the brain compensates as the vestibular nerve is slowly lost.
  • Larger tumours press on the trigeminal nerve (facial numbness, a reduced corneal reflex), the cerebellum (limb ataxia) and finally the fourth ventricle (hydrocephalus). The facial nerve tolerates stretching well, so facial weakness is a late finding.

Bilateral vestibular schwannomas define NF2-related schwannomatosis (formerly neurofibromatosis type 2). It is autosomal dominant, caused by loss of the NF2 tumour suppressor on chromosome 22, which encodes merlin, a protein linking the cytoskeleton to the cell membrane. Other features are meningiomas, ependymomas and juvenile posterior subcapsular cataracts.

Paraganglioma (glomus tumour)

A tumour of paraganglion chief cells, which derive from the neural crest. Nests of chief cells (chromogranin positive) are surrounded by S-100-positive sustentacular cells in a richly vascular stroma. In the ear it arises on the promontory (glomus tympanicum) or at the jugular bulb (glomus jugulare). Typical features:

  • Pulsatile tinnitus in time with the heartbeat, and conductive hearing loss;
  • a red-purple mass seen behind an intact eardrum;
  • with jugular foramen spread, palsies of cranial nerves IX, X and XI.

Up to about a third of head and neck paragangliomas are hereditary, most often from germline variants in a succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) subunit gene. SDH is complex II of the electron transport chain and also a citric acid cycle enzyme. Its loss lets succinate build up, which stabilises hypoxia-inducible factor. Never biopsy a suspected glomus tumour through the eardrum, because it bleeds briskly.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma and the adult with a one-sided effusion

A carcinoma in the lateral nasopharynx (the fossa of Rosenmüller) can block the eustachian tube opening. It then shows up as one-sided otitis media with effusion in an adult, sometimes with a neck node or nasal bleeding. The common non-keratinizing (undifferentiated) type is strongly linked to Epstein-Barr virus and is most frequent in southern China, Southeast Asia and North Africa.

Skin cancers of the auricle

The helix gets heavy sun exposure. Squamous cell carcinoma (keratin pearls; it can spread to the parotid and neck nodes) and basal cell carcinoma are both common. Ultraviolet B light creates pyrimidine (thymine) dimers, which are repaired by nucleotide excision repair. Xeroderma pigmentosum, a defect in that repair, causes skin cancers in childhood.

TumourKey clueCell or cause
Vestibular schwannomaOne-sided sensorineural loss and tinnitusSchwann cell; NF2 (merlin)
ParagangliomaPulsatile tinnitus, red mass behind the drumNeural crest chief cell; SDH genes
Nasopharyngeal carcinomaAdult with one-sided effusion, neck nodeEpithelial; Epstein-Barr virus
Auricular squamous cell carcinomaUlcerated helix lesion in sun-exposed older adultUltraviolet damage
Exam trap: in vestibular schwannoma the facial nerve sits right next to the tumour, yet a reduced corneal reflex usually comes before facial weakness.

s23e-s09a03.bodyHtml:
From air to nerve

  • Middle ear: the eardrum and ossicles match the low impedance of air to the high impedance of inner-ear fluid. The large drum drives the small stapes footplate, which concentrates force and lever action. Without this, most sound energy would bounce off the fluid.
  • Cochlea: the basilar membrane is narrow and stiff at the base and wide and floppy at the apex. High frequencies peak near the base and low frequencies near the apex (tonotopy). Noise, ageing and ototoxic drugs damage the basal hair cells first, so high tones go first.
  • Hair cells sit in endolymph, which is rich in potassium. The stria vascularis keeps it about +80 mV positive (the endocochlear potential). Bending the stereocilia opens mechanotransduction channels, and K+ flowing in depolarises the cell. Inner hair cells send signals to the brain. Outer hair cells change length (through the motor protein prestin) to amplify the signal; they generate otoacoustic emissions.
  • Supporting cells recycle K+ back to the stria through gap junctions made of connexins.

Conductive versus sensorineural

Conductive loss is a problem in the canal, drum or ossicles. Sensorineural loss is a problem in the cochlea, the cochlear nerve or the central pathways. The tuning-fork tests and the audiogram tell them apart.

CauseTypeDistinguishing feature
Cerumen, otitis media with effusionConductiveAbnormal otoscopy
OtosclerosisConductiveNormal drum; young adult, often female; abnormal bone remodelling fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window; worsens in pregnancy
PresbycusisSensorineuralBoth ears, high tones first; trouble following speech in noise
NoiseSensorineuralNotch near 4 kHz
Vestibular schwannomaSensorineural (retrocochlear)One-sided; speech understanding worse than the tone thresholds predict

Congenital and genetic hearing loss

  • Congenital cytomegalovirus is the most common non-genetic cause. The loss may be absent at birth and appear or worsen later. Look for periventricular calcifications, microcephaly and petechiae.
  • GJB2 (connexin 26) variants are the most common genetic cause of non-syndromic sensorineural loss. They are autosomal recessive, so the parents usually hear normally.
  • Pendred syndrome (autosomal recessive, SLC26A4, pendrin): sensorineural loss with an enlarged vestibular aqueduct, plus goitre. Pendrin moves iodide across the apical membrane of thyroid cells into the follicle, so organification is impaired.
  • Alport syndrome (usually X-linked, type IV collagen alpha-5 chain): haematuria that progresses to kidney failure, high-frequency sensorineural loss and anterior lenticonus.
  • Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome (autosomal recessive potassium-channel variants): congenital deafness with a long QT interval and a risk of sudden death.
  • Waardenburg syndrome (for example PAX3): deafness, a white forelock, heterochromia of the irises and widely spaced inner canthi, from a neural crest melanocyte defect.
Exam trap: in one-sided sensorineural loss, the Weber goes to the good ear and the Rinne stays positive (air louder than bone) on the bad side, just softer.

s23e-s09a04.bodyHtml:
Each labyrinth has three semicircular canals set at right angles. Their cristae sense angular acceleration, that is, head rotation. The two otolith organs, the utricle and the saccule, have maculae topped by calcium carbonate crystals (otoconia). They sense linear acceleration and head tilt relative to gravity. At rest both vestibular nerves fire tonically at equal rates. The brain reads a difference between the two sides as movement.

The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR)

When the head turns right, the right horizontal canal is excited and the eyes move left by the same amount, so gaze stays on target. If one labyrinth or vestibular nerve stops working:

  • The healthy side's tonic firing is unopposed, so the brain senses rotation towards the healthy side. The eyes drift slowly towards the damaged side, and quick corrective jerks beat away from the lesion. This is spontaneous horizontal-torsional nystagmus that fixation dampens.
  • The head impulse test is abnormal when the head is turned quickly towards the damaged side: the eyes move with the head, then make a catch-up saccade back to the target.
  • The patient tends to veer or fall towards the damaged side.

Peripheral disorders

DisorderMechanismTime courseHearing
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)Otoconia loosened from the utricle drift into a canal, most often the posterior canal (canalithiasis). They move with gravity when the head moves.Seconds, triggered by changes in head positionNormal
Vestibular neuritisInflammation of the vestibular nerve, probably viralContinuous vertigo for days, slow recoveryNormal
LabyrinthitisInflammation of the whole labyrinthContinuous for daysSensorineural loss
Ménière diseaseToo much endolymph (endolymphatic hydrops), linked to poor resorption in the endolymphatic sacAttacks lasting 20 minutes to 12 hoursFluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss, tinnitus, fullness

Central causes to keep in mind

A stroke of the cerebellum or brainstem can look like vestibular neuritis. Occlusion of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA), which usually supplies the labyrinthine artery, can cause sudden vertigo with one-sided deafness, facial weakness and limb ataxia on the same side. Nystagmus that changes direction with gaze, vertical or purely torsional nystagmus, and a vertical misalignment of the eyes (skew deviation) all point to a central cause.

Motion sickness and its drugs

Motion sickness comes from a conflict between vestibular, visual and body-position signals. Scopolamine, a muscarinic antagonist given as a patch behind the ear, and first-generation H1 antihistamines such as meclizine and dimenhydrinate act on vestibular and brainstem pathways. Scopolamine side effects are anticholinergic: dry mouth, drowsiness, confusion in older adults, urinary retention and dilated pupils. Dilated pupils can trigger angle-closure glaucoma in eyes with narrow angles.

Pearl: in a peripheral lesion the fast phase beats away from the bad ear, and a quick head turn towards the bad ear shows the catch-up saccade.

s23e-s09a05.bodyHtml:
Auricular haematoma

Auricular cartilage has no blood vessels of its own. It is fed by diffusion from the overlying perichondrium. A shearing blow (wrestling, boxing, rugby) bleeds into the space between cartilage and perichondrium. The cartilage loses its blood supply and dies, and the perichondrium lays down new, disorganised fibrocartilage. The result is a permanently thickened, crumpled ear ("cauliflower ear") unless the blood is drained early.

Tympanic membrane perforation

Causes include a slap or blast (a sudden pressure wave), cotton swabs or other objects, and AOM that ruptures. The eardrum is the structure most easily injured by a primary blast wave, because air-filled organs are the most vulnerable. Small traumatic perforations usually heal on their own. Vertigo or sensorineural loss after the injury suggests the inner ear was damaged as well.

Temporal bone fracture

These follow major head trauma. Signs of a fracture of the skull base include bruising over the mastoid (Battle sign), blood behind the eardrum (haemotympanum), and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) otorrhoea, or rhinorrhoea when the drum is intact and fluid drains down the eustachian tube. Beta-2 transferrin in the fluid confirms CSF, because this form of transferrin is made within the central nervous system.

PatternTypical result
Fracture that spares the otic capsule (most cases; older term: longitudinal, from a blow to the side of the head)Torn drum, haemotympanum, ossicular disruption: conductive loss. Facial nerve injury is less common.
Fracture that crosses the otic capsule (older term: transverse, from a blow to the front or back of the head)Sensorineural loss and vertigo from labyrinth damage. Facial nerve injury is more common.

Barotrauma

By Boyle's law, gas volume falls as pressure rises. During descent in an aircraft or a dive, the middle ear must be filled with air through the eustachian tube. If the tube stays shut (for example, with a cold), the relative vacuum pulls the eardrum inwards and causes pain, fluid or bleeding in the middle ear. The tube is opened by the tensor veli palatini, supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. Forceful Valsalva against a blocked tube can rupture the round or oval window. The resulting perilymph fistula causes sudden sensorineural loss and vertigo.

Foreign bodies

Button batteries are an emergency. Current flowing through moist tissue makes hydroxide ions at the negative pole, and this causes alkaline liquefactive necrosis within hours, even with a "dead" battery. Vegetable matter swells when wet, so it should not be irrigated.

Exam trap: clear fluid from the ear after head trauma is CSF until proven otherwise. Test for beta-2 transferrin; glucose testing is unreliable.

s23e-s09a06.bodyHtml:
Ototoxic drugs damage the cochlea, the vestibular system or both. Cochlear damage usually starts with the outer hair cells in the basal turn, so high frequencies go first. Patients often do not notice until the loss reaches speech frequencies. Vestibular damage is usually bilateral and symmetric, so it causes imbalance and blurred vision with head movement (oscillopsia), not spinning vertigo.

DrugMain targetMechanismReversible?
AminoglycosidesGentamicin and streptomycin mostly vestibular; amikacin, neomycin and kanamycin mostly cochlearTaken up into hair cells through mechanotransduction channels, form reactive oxygen species, trigger apoptosis; build up in inner-ear fluidsNo (permanent)
CisplatinCochlea (outer hair cells, stria vascularis)Reactive oxygen species and DNA damage; dose-related; children at highest riskNo
Loop diuretics (furosemide, ethacrynic acid)CochleaBlock the Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter (NKCC1) in the stria vascularis, so the endocochlear potential collapses; worst with fast high-dose IV doses and kidney failureUsually
Salicylates (high dose)CochleaInterfere with outer hair cell electromotility (prestin); tinnitus and mild lossYes, within days of stopping
Quinine, chloroquine, hydroxychloroquineCochleaCinchonism: tinnitus, hearing loss, headache, blurred vision, nauseaOften, but not always

Aminoglycosides in more depth

The risk rises with total dose and duration, high trough levels, kidney impairment, older age, and loop diuretics or other ototoxins given at the same time. A maternally inherited variant in the mitochondrial 12S ribosomal RNA gene (MT-RNR1, m.1555A>G) makes the mitochondrial ribosome look more like a bacterial one. In carriers, even a single standard dose can cause profound, permanent deafness. Because the variant is mitochondrial, it passes from a mother to all her children, and affected relatives are on the mother's side.

Pearl: aminoglycoside ototoxicity can begin or progress after the drug is stopped, because the drug stays in inner-ear fluids for a long time.
Exam trap: a patient on gentamicin who complains that the world bounces while walking has bilateral vestibular loss. There may be no vertigo and normal hearing.

s23e-s09b01.bodyHtml:
Acute otitis media: diagnosis

Diagnose AOM when the eardrum is moderately or severely bulging, or there is new ear discharge not caused by otitis externa. Mild bulging counts if there is recent ear pain (in a non-verbal child: holding, tugging or rubbing the ear) or intense redness of the drum. Do not diagnose AOM without middle-ear fluid; pneumatic otoscopy shows reduced drum movement.

Antibiotics or observation (children aged 6 months and older)

PresentationApproach
Severe signs (moderate or severe pain, pain for 48 hours or more, or temperature 39°C (102.2°F) or higher), or ear dischargeAntibiotics at any age
Age 6 to 23 months, both ears, not severeAntibiotics
Age 6 to 23 months, one ear, not severeAntibiotics or observation, decided with the family
Age 2 years or older, not severeAntibiotics or observation, decided with the family

Observation means pain relief now and a reliable plan to start antibiotics if the child is not better, or is worse, by 48 to 72 hours. Treat the pain in every case (acetaminophen or ibuprofen).

  • First line: high-dose amoxicillin.
  • Amoxicillin-clavulanate instead if amoxicillin was taken in the past 30 days, if there is purulent conjunctivitis too (suggesting beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae), or if amoxicillin has failed.
  • Penicillin allergy that is not immediate-type: an oral cephalosporin such as cefdinir, cefuroxime or cefpodoxime. Intramuscular ceftriaxone is used when oral treatment fails or is not possible.
  • Reassess at 48 to 72 hours if symptoms persist. Consider tympanostomy tubes for recurrent AOM (3 episodes in 6 months, or 4 in a year with 1 in the past 6 months) when middle-ear fluid is present at the assessment.

Otitis media with effusion (OME)

Fluid without signs of acute infection. Most cases clear within 3 months, so watch and wait, and recheck every 3 to 6 months. Antibiotics, corticosteroids, antihistamines and decongestants do not help. Test hearing if the fluid lasts 3 months or more. Offer tympanostomy tubes for fluid in both ears for 3 months or more with documented hearing loss, or sooner in children at risk of speech or learning delay. For discharge through a tube, use topical antibiotic drops (a fluoroquinolone) rather than oral antibiotics.

Otitis externa

  • Uncomplicated: topical antibiotic drops, with or without a corticosteroid, for about 7 days. Insert a wick if the canal is too swollen for drops to get in. Keep the ear dry and give pain relief. Oral antibiotics are not needed.
  • If the drum is perforated, or a tube is in place, use a non-ototoxic fluoroquinolone drop, not an aminoglycoside drop.
  • Give systemic antibiotics only if infection spreads beyond the canal, or in diabetes or immune compromise.

Necrotizing otitis externa (an older adult with diabetes, severe pain, granulation tissue on the canal floor, a raised ESR, and sometimes facial palsy): image the temporal bone (CT shows bone erosion; MRI shows soft-tissue and intracranial spread). Send a culture, start IV antipseudomonal antibiotics for weeks, control the glucose, and involve ENT.

Complications

  • Acute mastoiditis: swelling, redness and tenderness behind the ear, with the auricle pushed forwards. Give IV antibiotics. Order contrast CT of the temporal bones for an abscess or intracranial spread. Myringotomy, with or without a tube, drains the middle ear; mastoidectomy is for abscess or failed treatment.
  • Cholesteatoma: painless, foul discharge that keeps coming back, a retraction pocket with white debris, and conductive loss. Treatment is surgical removal. Drops only calm the infection on top.
  • Ramsay Hunt syndrome: facial palsy plus vesicles in the ear. Give an oral corticosteroid plus an antiviral (valacyclovir or acyclovir) early, and protect the eye.
Exam trap: fluid behind the drum weeks after AOM, in a well child, is OME. It does not need another course of antibiotics.

s23e-s09b02.bodyHtml:
Asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss or one-sided tinnitus

A meaningful difference in sensorineural loss between the ears, or one-sided tinnitus, needs a look for a retrocochlear lesion. The test of choice is gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canals. CT can miss small intracanalicular tumours.

Vestibular schwannoma: choosing treatment

OptionBest for
Observation with serial MRISmall, slow-growing tumours, especially in older patients or those with other illnesses (many never grow)
Stereotactic radiosurgerySmall to medium tumours that are growing
Microsurgical removalLarge tumours compressing the brainstem, or younger patients choosing removal

Bilateral tumours, or a tumour in a young person, prompt evaluation for NF2-related schwannomatosis. That means an eye exam for juvenile cataract, spinal imaging, genetic counselling and screening of relatives.

Pulsatile tinnitus

Rhythmic, pulse-synchronous tinnitus needs otoscopy and vascular imaging. A red mass behind an intact drum suggests a paraganglioma: image with CT of the temporal bone and MRI. Do not biopsy through the eardrum. Before surgery, check plasma free metanephrines, because a few of these tumours secrete catecholamines. Other causes include idiopathic intracranial hypertension, dural arteriovenous fistula, arterial stenosis or dissection, and a high-output state such as anaemia or thyrotoxicosis.

The adult with one-sided otitis media with effusion

OME is common in children but unusual in adults. New, persistent fluid on one side, especially with a neck mass, nosebleeds or nasal blockage, or in someone from a high-incidence region, needs endoscopic examination of the nasopharynx, with biopsy of any mass, to exclude nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is treated mainly with radiotherapy, with chemotherapy for advanced stages.

Lesions of the auricle

A non-healing, crusted or ulcerated lesion on the helix of an older, sun-exposed patient needs a biopsy before any destructive treatment. Excise squamous and basal cell carcinomas with clear margins (Mohs surgery spares cartilage). Examine the parotid and neck nodes.

Exam trap: do not treat an adult's one-sided effusion with antibiotics or a tube alone. Look at the nasopharynx first.

s23e-s09b03.bodyHtml:
Newborns

Every newborn is screened, with otoacoustic emissions or automated auditory brainstem response (ABR). The 1-3-6 timeline: screen by 1 month, confirm a loss with a full diagnostic audiological evaluation (diagnostic ABR) by 3 months, and start intervention (hearing aids, early intervention services) by 6 months. Babies in the neonatal intensive care unit are screened with ABR, because emissions miss auditory neuropathy. A failed screen is never "probably fluid" without a diagnostic follow-up.

Congenital cytomegalovirus: test saliva or urine by PCR within the first 3 weeks of life (later positives may reflect postnatal infection). Newborns with symptomatic disease are treated with oral valganciclovir for 6 months, which improves hearing and developmental outcomes. They need repeated hearing tests, because the loss can be delayed or progressive.

Children

Test hearing in any child with speech delay, school difficulties or persistent effusion. Cochlear implants are an option for severe to profound sensorineural loss from about 9 to 12 months of age. Earlier implantation gives better language outcomes.

Adults: a stepwise approach

  1. Otoscopy: cerumen, effusion, perforation, cholesteatoma.
  2. Tuning forks (Weber, Rinne) to separate conductive from sensorineural loss.
  3. Formal audiometry.
  4. MRI of the internal auditory canals if the sensorineural loss is asymmetric.
ConditionManagement
Cerumen impactionSoftening drops, irrigation (only if the drum is known to be intact), or manual removal
PresbycusisAudiology referral and hearing aids (over-the-counter aids are an option for mild to moderate loss); cochlear implant when aids no longer help. Treating hearing loss may lower the risk of cognitive decline.
Noise-induced lossPrevention: hearing protection and less exposure. In the workplace, an average of 85 dBA over 8 hours triggers a hearing conservation program.
OtosclerosisHearing aid, or surgery (stapedotomy or stapedectomy)

Sudden sensorineural hearing loss: an otologic urgency

A sensorineural loss of 30 dB or more at 3 neighbouring frequencies, developing within 72 hours, usually in one ear. Most cases have no cause found. A patient who "wakes up deaf in one ear" is often wrongly told it is wax or fluid.

  • First separate it from a conductive loss: tuning forks in the room, then audiometry promptly.
  • Do not order routine blood tests or CT.
  • Offer a corticosteroid (oral, or intratympanic injection) as early as possible, ideally within 2 weeks. Intratympanic steroid is a salvage option if recovery is incomplete. Hyperbaric oxygen can be added within 3 months.
  • Get an MRI of the internal auditory canals (or ABR if MRI is not possible) to look for a retrocochlear lesion such as vestibular schwannoma.
  • Sudden loss with vertigo and other brainstem signs can be an AICA stroke. Send the patient straight to emergency stroke imaging.
Exam trap: antivirals, antibiotics and "watch for a week" are wrong answers for sudden sensorineural loss. Confirm it with an audiogram and start steroids early.

s23e-s09b04.bodyHtml:
Sort vertigo by timing and trigger more than by how the patient describes it.

PatternCommon peripheral causeDangerous mimic
Brief (seconds to under a minute), set off by changes in head positionBPPVCentral positional nystagmus (posterior fossa lesion)
Acute and continuous for a day or more, with nausea, nystagmus and unsteady gait (acute vestibular syndrome)Vestibular neuritis; labyrinthitis if hearing is lostCerebellar or brainstem stroke
Spontaneous attacks lasting minutes to hoursMénière disease; vestibular migraineTransient ischaemic attack of the posterior circulation

BPPV

The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre brings on vertigo and torsional upbeating nystagmus towards the lower ear, after a short delay. It lasts under a minute and lessens with repeated tests. Treat with canalith repositioning (the Epley manoeuvre) on the affected side. No imaging, no lab tests and no routine vestibular suppressants are needed, and there is no need to restrict posture after the manoeuvre. If BPPV is suspected but the Dix-Hallpike is negative, test the horizontal canal with a supine roll test. BPPV is common in older adults and raises their risk of falls, so ask about it.

Acute vestibular syndrome: peripheral or stroke?

In a patient with ongoing vertigo and nystagmus, a three-part bedside exam (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew) is more sensitive for stroke than early CT, or even early diffusion MRI.

  • Reassuring (peripheral): an abnormal head impulse test (a catch-up saccade), nystagmus in one direction only, and no skew deviation.
  • Dangerous (central): a normal head impulse test in a patient who has nystagmus, nystagmus that changes direction with gaze, or skew deviation. New hearing loss also raises concern for an AICA infarct.
  • Central signs, severe imbalance (cannot stand or walk unaided), or vascular risk factors with a new headache: get an MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging, and repeat it if the first is negative but suspicion remains. Noncontrast CT misses most posterior fossa infarcts.

Vestibular neuritis: a short course of a vestibular suppressant (meclizine, or a benzodiazepine) for the first days only, antiemetics, then early mobilisation and vestibular rehabilitation. Long-term suppressants slow the brain's compensation.

Ménière disease

The diagnosis needs 2 or more attacks of vertigo, each lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, with low- to mid-frequency sensorineural loss documented on audiometry in that ear, and fluctuating hearing, tinnitus or fullness in it. Rule out a vestibular schwannoma with MRI.

  • Maintenance: education, less dietary salt, and limiting caffeine and alcohol; a diuretic can be added.
  • Attacks: a short-term vestibular suppressant or antiemetic.
  • Persistent attacks: intratympanic corticosteroid. Then destructive options for the vertigo, which may cost hearing: intratympanic gentamicin, surgery to the endolymphatic sac, labyrinthectomy or vestibular nerve section.

Vestibular migraine

Recurrent vestibular attacks lasting 5 minutes to 72 hours in someone with migraine, with migraine features (headache, light or sound sensitivity, aura) during at least half of the attacks. Hearing is normal between attacks. Manage it as migraine: identify triggers, treat attacks, and use preventives for frequent episodes.

Motion sickness

Prevent it with a transdermal scopolamine patch applied behind the ear several hours before travel, or with a first-generation antihistamine (meclizine, dimenhydrinate). Avoid scopolamine in narrow-angle glaucoma, urinary retention and, where possible, in frail older adults (it can cause delirium). Behavioural measures help too: look at the horizon, and sit where motion is least.

Exam trap: a normal head impulse test is reassuring in a patient who is not dizzy. In a patient with acute, continuous vertigo and nystagmus, it suggests stroke.

s23e-s09b05.bodyHtml:
Auricular haematoma

A tense, fluctuant, purple swelling on the front of the auricle after a blow. Treat promptly by incision and drainage (or needle aspiration if it is small and fresh), then a bolster or compressive dressing to stop it filling again. Review within a day or so, because it often recurs. Leaving it causes cartilage necrosis and cauliflower ear. Advise protective headgear for contact sports.

Traumatic tympanic membrane perforation

  • Most heal on their own within weeks. Keep water out of the ear and avoid ototoxic (aminoglycoside) drops. Antibiotic drops (a fluoroquinolone) are used only for contamination or infection. Check healing and hearing with audiometry at follow-up.
  • Refer for repair (tympanoplasty) if it has not healed after about 2 to 3 months.
  • Refer urgently for vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss or facial weakness after the injury, which point to inner-ear injury or a perilymph fistula.

Temporal bone fracture

Assess the patient first as a head-injury patient (airway, cervical spine, CT of the head). High-resolution CT of the temporal bones defines the fracture. Check facial nerve function as early as possible, because the timing of a palsy matters:

  • Delayed-onset or incomplete facial weakness (swelling in the canal): an excellent prognosis. Give an oral corticosteroid and observe.
  • Immediate, complete paralysis (nerve cut or crushed): electrodiagnostic testing and surgical decompression or exploration are considered.

CSF otorrhoea: most leaks stop with conservative care. Keep the head of the bed up, tell the patient not to strain or blow the nose, and give stool softeners. Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended. Persistent leaks need a lumbar drain or surgical repair. Do not pack the canal, and do not put drops in an ear that is leaking CSF.

Barotrauma

Middle-ear barotrauma (ear pain after flying or diving, a retracted or bruised drum, mild conductive loss) is managed with pain relief and decongestants, and no flying or diving until the ear is normal. Advise against diving with a cold, and suggest equalising early and often. Vertigo or sensorineural loss after a dive needs urgent evaluation. It may be inner-ear barotrauma, which needs rest and no further diving, or inner-ear decompression sickness, which needs hyperbaric oxygen.

Foreign bodies in the ear

ObjectApproach
Button batteryRemove immediately, under direct vision or a microscope. Do not irrigate. Check the canal and drum afterwards for burns.
Live insectKill it first with mineral oil or lidocaine drops, then remove it
Food or plant matterDo not irrigate (it swells). Remove with forceps or suction.
Small, smooth inert objectIrrigation or instruments, if the drum is intact and the child is still. Refer to ENT if removal fails or the child cannot cooperate.
Exam trap: a button battery in the ear or nose is not a clinic appointment. It is a same-hour removal, like one in the oesophagus.

s23e-s09b06.bodyHtml:
Before treatment

  • Ask about personal or family hearing loss, especially deafness after an aminoglycoside in a maternal relative. This suggests the mitochondrial MT-RNR1 m.1555A>G variant. In known carriers, avoid aminoglycosides unless no adequate alternative exists for a life-threatening infection.
  • Get a baseline audiogram (including high frequencies) before long courses of aminoglycosides, for example for drug-resistant tuberculosis or nontuberculous mycobacteria, and before cisplatin.
  • Adjust the dose for kidney function, use extended-interval dosing where it fits, and monitor drug levels.
  • Avoid giving other ototoxins at the same time where possible: loop diuretics and vancomycin with aminoglycosides.

During treatment

  • Repeat audiometry during prolonged courses, and ask about tinnitus, fullness, unsteadiness and oscillopsia.
  • New ototoxic symptoms on an aminoglycoside: stop the drug if an effective alternative exists, check levels and kidney function, and arrange audiological and vestibular testing. Damage is usually permanent, so early detection is what saves hearing.
DrugPractical point
Cisplatin in childrenMonitor hearing at each cycle. Sodium thiosulfate, given about 6 hours after cisplatin, lowers the risk of hearing loss in children with localised, non-metastatic solid tumours.
IV furosemideThe risk rises with high peak levels. Give large doses as a slow infusion (often quoted as no faster than about 4 mg/min), especially in kidney failure.
Aspirin and other salicylatesTinnitus at high doses: check a salicylate level and lower or stop the dose. Hearing recovers.
QuinineNot recommended for leg cramps. It can cause cinchonism and serious blood toxicity (thrombocytopenia, haemolytic-uraemic syndrome).
HydroxychloroquineHearing symptoms are uncommon. Retinal screening is the main monitoring.

Recognising vestibulotoxicity

Bilateral vestibular loss causes unsteadiness that is worse in the dark or on uneven ground, and oscillopsia on walking. The head impulse test is abnormal in both directions, and the Romberg test is positive. Patients need vestibular rehabilitation and fall-prevention measures.

Pearl: deafness after a single dose of gentamicin, with similar stories in the mother's relatives, points to a mitochondrial susceptibility variant. Record it as a lifelong drug alert.

s23e-s10a01.bodyHtml:
Psychosis means losing contact with reality: delusions (fixed false beliefs that do not yield to evidence), hallucinations (perceptions without a stimulus, most often voices in primary psychotic illness), disorganised speech or behaviour, and catatonia. Negative symptoms (flat affect, poverty of speech, loss of motivation and pleasure, social withdrawal) and cognitive deficits often matter more for long-term function, and they respond poorly to medication.

Neurobiology

  • Dopamine: too much dopamine signalling in the mesolimbic pathway is linked to positive symptoms, and too little in the mesocortical pathway to negative and cognitive symptoms. Every licensed antipsychotic blocks D2 receptors to some degree.
  • Glutamate: NMDA-receptor antagonists such as phencyclidine and ketamine reproduce both positive and negative symptoms, supporting an NMDA hypofunction model.
  • Structure: enlarged lateral and third ventricles, reduced cortical and hippocampal volume, and fewer dendritic spines on cortical pyramidal neurons.
  • Risk factors: a first-degree relative (risk rises steeply with genetic closeness; identical twins are concordant in well under 100%), 22q11.2 deletion, heavy cannabis use in adolescence, older paternal age, obstetric complications, migration and urban upbringing.

Antipsychotic drugs by mechanism

GroupExamplesReceptor profileSignature adverse effects
First-generation, high potencyHaloperidol, fluphenazineStrong D2 blockadeExtrapyramidal effects, high prolactin, neuroleptic malignant syndrome

s23e-s10a02.bodyHtml:
Fear is a normal response to present danger; anxiety is anticipation of a future threat. Disorders arise when either is out of proportion, persistent and disabling. The amygdala drives fear responses and fear learning; the medial prefrontal cortex normally damps it, and this top-down control is weak in anxiety disorders and PTSD. The locus coeruleus (noradrenaline) produces the arousal and autonomic surge of panic, and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis links chronic stress to the body.

Recognising the disorders

DisorderCore featureMinimum duration
Generalized anxiety disorderExcessive, hard-to-control worry about many things, with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension or poor sleep6 months
Panic disorderRecurrent unexpected panic attacks, then a month or more of worry about further attacks or avoidance1 month after an attack
AgoraphobiaFear of places where escape or help would be hard (transport, open or enclosed spaces, crowds, being outside alone)6 months
Specific phobiaFear of one object or situation (animals, heights, injections)6 months
Social anxiety disorderFear of scrutiny or embarrassment in social or performance settings6 months
Obsessive-compulsive disorderIntrusive, unwanted thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive acts done to reduce the distress (compulsions); insight variesNo minimum; time-consuming or impairing
Posttraumatic stress disorderAfter a trauma: intrusions, avoidance, negative changes in thinking and mood, and hyperarousalMore than 1 month
Acute stress disorderThe same picture soon after the trauma3 days to 1 month
Adjustment disorderDistress or impairment out of proportion to an identifiable non-traumatic stressorBegins within 3 months; ends within 6 months of the stressor ending

The obsessive-compulsive spectrum also includes body dysmorphic disorder (preoccupation with a perceived flaw in appearance), hoarding disorder, trichotillomania (hair pulling) and excoriation (skin picking). OCD is linked to overactivity of cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops, especially orbitofrontal cortex and caudate.

Drugs by mechanism

  • SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line for most of these disorders. Benefit builds over weeks; OCD usually needs higher doses and longer trials. Clomipramine, a serotonergic tricyclic, is an older alternative for OCD.
  • Benzodiazepines bind between the alpha and gamma subunits of the GABA-A receptor and increase the frequency of chloride-channel opening. Barbiturates instead increase the duration of opening and can open the channel directly at high doses, so they are far more dangerous in overdose. Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine site.
  • Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist for generalized anxiety: no sedation, no dependence, no cross-tolerance with alcohol, but it takes weeks to work and does not abort panic.
  • Propranolol blunts the peripheral adrenergic symptoms (tremor, palpitations) of performance anxiety.
  • Hydroxyzine, an H1 antihistamine, is a non-addictive sedating option.
Exam trap: benzodiazepines plus alcohol or opioids depress breathing more than either alone. Long-acting benzodiazepines accumulate in older adults and raise the risk of falls and confusion.
High-yield: before diagnosing panic disorder, think of hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, stimulant or caffeine use, and alcohol or sedative withdrawal.

s23e-s10a03.bodyHtml:
A major depressive episode is at least 2 weeks of depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure, with enough other symptoms (sleep, appetite or weight change, psychomotor change, fatigue, guilt or worthlessness, poor concentration, thoughts of death) to total five or more. A manic episode is at least 1 week (or any length if hospitalisation is needed) of abnormally elevated or irritable mood with more energy, plus symptoms such as grandiosity, less need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, distractibility and risky behaviour, causing marked impairment. Hypomania is the same picture for at least 4 days without marked impairment or psychosis.

Biology

  • Monoamine deficits (serotonin, noradrenaline, dopamine) explain how antidepressants were found, but the weeks-long delay in their benefit points to downstream changes in receptor sensitivity, neuroplasticity and BDNF signalling.
  • The HPA axis is often overactive in depression: high cortisol and failure to suppress it with dexamethasone.
  • Sleep in depression: shorter REM latency, more REM early in the night, less slow-wave sleep and early-morning waking.
  • Bipolar disorder is among the most heritable psychiatric disorders.

Antidepressants

ClassMechanismNotable adverse effects
SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram, paroxetine)Block the serotonin transporterSexual dysfunction, GI upset, hyponatraemia from SIADH (older adults), bleeding risk with NSAIDs or anticoagulants, QT prolongation with higher citalopram doses, discontinuation symptoms (worst with paroxetine)
SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine, desvenlafaxine)Block serotonin and noradrenaline transportersAs SSRIs, plus dose-related hypertension; duloxetine also treats neuropathic pain
BupropionInhibits noradrenaline and dopamine reuptakeLowers the seizure threshold (avoid in eating disorders and seizure disorders); no sexual dysfunction or weight gain; also aids smoking cessation
MirtazapineAlpha-2 antagonist that increases noradrenaline and serotonin release; strong H1 blockadeSedation, increased appetite and weight gain
Trazodone5-HT2A antagonist with weak reuptake inhibitionSedation (used for insomnia), orthostasis, priapism
Tricyclics (amitriptyline, nortriptyline, clomipramine)Block serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake; also block muscarinic, H1, alpha-1 and cardiac sodium channelsAnticholinergic effects, orthostasis; in overdose, wide QRS, arrhythmia, seizures and coma
MAO inhibitors (phenelzine, tranylcypromine, selegiline patch)Irreversibly inhibit monoamine oxidaseHypertensive crisis with tyramine-rich foods; serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs
Esketamine (nasal)NMDA receptor antagonistDissociation, sedation, raised blood pressure; given under observation
Zuranolone, brexanoloneNeuroactive steroids; positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A receptorsSedation; used for postpartum depression

Tyramine is normally broken down by MAO-A in the gut wall and liver. When MAO is blocked, it reaches sympathetic nerve endings and releases stored noradrenaline, causing a sudden severe rise in blood pressure.

Mood stabilisers

  • Lithium inhibits inositol monophosphatase (depleting inositol for phosphoinositide signalling) and glycogen synthase kinase-3. It has a narrow therapeutic range and is cleared unchanged by the kidney, reabsorbed like sodium in the proximal tubule. Anything that makes the kidney hold on to sodium (thiazides, dehydration, low-salt diet, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors) raises lithium levels. Adverse effects: tremor, hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (lithium enters collecting-duct principal cells through ENaC; amiloride blocks this), hypercalcaemia from hyperparathyroidism, chronic kidney disease, and a small rise in the risk of Ebstein anomaly with first-trimester exposure.
  • Valproate: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, weight gain, thrombocytopenia, and a high risk of neural tube defects and lower IQ in exposed children.
  • Lamotrigine prevents depressive relapse; titrate slowly because of Stevens-Johnson syndrome; valproate doubles its level.
  • Carbamazepine: agranulocytosis, SIADH, liver enzyme induction, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome linked to HLA-B*15:02.
Exam trap: an antidepressant given alone to someone with unrecognised bipolar disorder can switch them into mania. Ask about past elevated-mood episodes and family history first.
High-yield: serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, sweating, diarrhoea, fever) develops within about a day of adding or raising a serotonergic drug; treat by stopping the drugs, giving benzodiazepines and, if needed, cyproheptadine (a 5-HT2A antagonist).

s23e-s10b01.bodyHtml:
Telling the psychotic disorders apart

DiagnosisKey features
Brief psychotic disorderPsychotic symptoms for more than 1 day and less than 1 month, then full return to previous function; often after a severe stressor or after childbirth
Schizophreniform disorderSchizophrenia-like illness lasting 1 to 6 months
SchizophreniaTwo or more of delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised or catatonic behaviour and negative symptoms (at least one of the first three) for at least 1 month, with continuous signs for at least 6 months and a fall in function
Schizoaffective disorderMood episodes present for most of the illness, plus at least 2 weeks of delusions or hallucinations with no mood episode
Delusional disorderOne or more delusions for at least 1 month; behaviour and function otherwise largely preserved; no prominent hallucinations or disorganisation
Mood disorder with psychotic featuresPsychosis occurs only during depressive or manic episodes

First episode: exclude other causes

  • History of substances (stimulants, cannabis, hallucinogens, phencyclidine), prescribed drugs (corticosteroids, levodopa, high-dose anticholinergics) and alcohol withdrawal.
  • Look for delirium: fluctuating attention and consciousness point to a medical cause, not a primary psychosis.
  • Basic tests: blood count, electrolytes, glucose, kidney and liver function, TSH, urine drug screen, HIV and syphilis testing. Brain imaging, EEG or lumbar puncture when there are neurological signs, an atypical course, older age at onset or confusion (for example, anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis).

Treatment

  • A second-generation antipsychotic at the lowest effective dose, chosen by side-effect profile, plus psychoeducation, family support, supported employment and cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis. Coordinated specialty care for a first episode improves outcomes.
  • Baseline and follow-up monitoring: weight or BMI, waist, blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids; ECG when the drug or patient raises QT risk; prolactin if symptoms appear; regular checks for abnormal movements.
  • Long-acting injectables (for example, paliperidone, aripiprazole, haloperidol or fluphenazine preparations) help when adherence is poor or relapses follow stopping medication.
  • Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (no adequate response to two antipsychotics given at an adequate dose and duration) calls for clozapine. Clozapine is also the drug that lowers suicidal behaviour in schizophrenia. The absolute neutrophil count is measured before starting and regularly during treatment; watch for fever and chest pain in the first weeks (myocarditis), constipation, sialorrhoea and seizures.
  • Acute agitation: verbal de-escalation first; then an oral or intramuscular antipsychotic, often with a benzodiazepine (but avoid parenteral olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepines).

Emergencies

SyndromeCluesManagement
Neuroleptic malignant syndromeDays after starting or raising a dopamine blocker (or stopping a dopamine agonist): fever, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion, unstable blood pressure and pulse, very high creatine kinase, raised white countStop the drug; cooling, IV fluids, ICU care; benzodiazepines; dantrolene or bromocriptine in severe cases
CatatoniaMutism, posturing, staring, rigidity, negativism, waxy flexibilityLorazepam challenge and treatment; ECT if benzodiazepines fail or the patient is in danger
Exam trap: a patient who became confused and febrile after receiving haloperidol needs the drug stopped. Giving more antipsychotic for "worsening agitation" can be fatal.

s23e-s10b02.bodyHtml:
General approach

  • Screen for medical and substance causes: hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, asthma or COPD drugs, caffeine, stimulants, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. A TSH and, where symptoms suggest it, an ECG are reasonable.
  • Ask about depression, substance use and suicidal thinking, which often coexist.
  • First-line treatment for most disorders is cognitive behavioural therapy, an SSRI or SNRI, or both. Start low (anxious patients are sensitive to early jitteriness), increase to an effective dose, and continue for 6 to 12 months after response before a slow taper.
DisorderPreferred treatmentNotes
Generalized anxietyCBT and/or SSRI or SNRIBuspirone is an alternative or add-on; avoid long-term benzodiazepines
Panic disorderCBT and/or SSRI or SNRIA short benzodiazepine course can bridge the first weeks in selected patients without substance use
Specific phobiaExposure-based CBTMedication has little role
Social anxietyCBT and/or SSRI or SNRIPropranolol before a performance helps the performance-only form
OCDExposure and response prevention and/or an SSRI, often at higher dosesClomipramine or antipsychotic augmentation for partial response
Body dysmorphic disorderCBT and/or SSRICosmetic procedures rarely help and often worsen the preoccupation
PTSDTrauma-focused psychotherapy (prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, EMDR)SSRI (sertraline, paroxetine) or venlafaxine if therapy is unavailable or not enough; benzodiazepines are not recommended
Adjustment disorderSupportive or problem-focused psychotherapyMedication only for specific symptoms

Children and adolescents

  • Separation anxiety disorder (excessive distress at separation from attachment figures, refusing school, fear of harm to parents) lasting at least 4 weeks in children: CBT with parent involvement first; an SSRI for moderate to severe cases.
  • Selective mutism: consistent failure to speak in specific social settings despite speaking elsewhere.
  • SSRIs carry a boxed warning for suicidal thinking in people under 25; monitor closely after starting.

Benzodiazepines: when and how

  • Use them only short-term and avoid them in older adults, people with substance use disorders, sleep apnoea, or those taking opioids.
  • After long-term use, taper gradually; abrupt stopping can cause rebound anxiety, insomnia, tremor and seizures.
Exam trap: after a trauma, routine single-session debriefing does not prevent PTSD. Offer support, watch for persistent symptoms, and start trauma-focused therapy when acute stress disorder or PTSD develops.

s23e-s10b03.bodyHtml:
Diagnosis

  • Screen with a brief questionnaire (for example, the PHQ-2 then PHQ-9) and confirm with an interview.
  • Check TSH, a blood count and other tests guided by the history; review medicines and alcohol use.
  • Always ask about past mania or hypomania and family history of bipolar disorder.
DisorderDistinguishing feature
Major depressive disorderOne or more major depressive episodes, no mania or hypomania ever
Persistent depressive disorderDepressed mood most days for at least 2 years (1 year in children and adolescents)
Premenstrual dysphoric disorderMood symptoms in the week before menses that improve within days of onset of menses, confirmed by prospective daily ratings over at least two cycles
Seasonal patternEpisodes that regularly begin and remit at particular times of year
BereavementWaves of grief tied to reminders, self-esteem preserved; consider depression when worthlessness, pervasive anhedonia or suicidal intent appear

Treatment steps

  1. Mild depression: psychotherapy (CBT, interpersonal therapy, behavioural activation) or an antidepressant.
  2. Moderate to severe: an antidepressant plus psychotherapy. SSRIs are usually first; choose by side-effect profile (for example, mirtazapine for poor sleep and weight loss; bupropion when sexual side effects matter).
  3. Assess response after 4 to 8 weeks at an adequate dose. If response is partial, optimise the dose, then switch or augment (a second-generation antipsychotic such as aripiprazole, lithium, bupropion or mirtazapine).
  4. Continue for at least 6 to 12 months after remission; longer (often indefinitely) after recurrent episodes.
  5. Treatment-resistant depression: esketamine, ECT or other neuromodulation such as transcranial magnetic stimulation.

ECT is the most effective acute treatment for severe depression. It is preferred when depression has psychotic features, catatonia, refusal to eat or drink, or a high suicide risk that needs rapid response, and it is safe in pregnancy. The main adverse effects are transient confusion and memory loss around the treatment period.

Peripartum and premenstrual

  • Postpartum blues (tearfulness, mood lability in the first days, gone within 2 weeks): reassure and watch.
  • Depression with peripartum onset (in pregnancy or the weeks after delivery): psychotherapy, an SSRI (sertraline is commonly used in breastfeeding), or zuranolone, a 14-day oral course for postpartum depression.
  • Postpartum psychosis (confusion, delusions, often bipolar-related) is an emergency: admit, ensure the infant's safety, and treat.
  • PMDD: SSRIs (continuously or in the luteal phase only) or a combined oral contraceptive containing drospirenone.

Children, adolescents and older adults

  • Adolescents: CBT or interpersonal therapy; fluoxetine or escitalopram for moderate to severe depression, with close follow-up for emerging suicidal thinking.
  • Older adults: depression can present as cognitive complaints ("pseudodementia"); start antidepressants at low doses, check sodium on SSRIs, and avoid tricyclics and paroxetine (anticholinergic load).

Suicide risk

  • Ask directly about thoughts, plans, intent, preparation and access to means. Asking does not raise risk.
  • Strongest predictor: a previous attempt. Other factors: male sex, older age, living alone, chronic illness or pain, substance use, recent discharge from psychiatric care, and access to firearms.
  • High imminent risk (a plan with intent, or a recent serious attempt): keep the patient safe and admit, involuntarily if needed. Lower risk: a written safety plan, removal or locking of lethal means, treatment of the underlying disorder and early follow-up.
Exam trap: new energy in the first weeks of antidepressant treatment, before mood lifts, can make it easier to act on suicidal thoughts. Schedule early review.

s23e-s10b04.bodyHtml:
Diagnosis

  • Bipolar I: at least one manic episode. Bipolar II: at least one hypomanic and one major depressive episode, never mania. Cyclothymic disorder: at least 2 years (1 in young people) of many hypomanic and depressive symptoms that never meet episode criteria.
  • Exclude stimulants, corticosteroids, hyperthyroidism and frontal lobe lesions when mania appears for the first time, especially in later life.

Acute mania

  • Stop any antidepressant.
  • First line: lithium, valproate or a second-generation antipsychotic; in severe mania, an antipsychotic combined with lithium or valproate.
  • Agitation: an antipsychotic with or without a benzodiazepine. ECT for refractory or dangerous mania.
  • Admission when the patient is a danger to self or others or cannot care for themselves.

Bipolar depression

  • Evidence-based options: quetiapine, lurasidone, lumateperone, cariprazine, an olanzapine-fluoxetine combination, or lithium. Lamotrigine is useful mainly for preventing depressive relapse because it must be titrated slowly.
  • Avoid antidepressant monotherapy: it can trigger mania or rapid cycling.

Maintenance and lithium safety

  • Lithium lowers relapse and suicide risk. Before starting, check kidney function, TSH, calcium, a pregnancy test where relevant and an ECG if there is cardiac disease. Recheck levels 5 days after a change (about 12 hours after the last dose), then kidney function and TSH periodically.
  • Interactions that raise lithium levels: thiazides, ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers, NSAIDs, dehydration, vomiting and diarrhoea, low-salt diets.
  • Toxicity: GI upset, coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, confusion, myoclonus, seizures; chronic toxicity can occur at only modestly raised levels. Stop lithium, give IV saline, avoid nephrotoxins; activated charcoal does not bind lithium. Whole-bowel irrigation can help after a large sustained-release ingestion. Haemodialysis for severe neurological toxicity or very high levels, especially with poor kidney function.
  • Pregnancy: plan ahead. Valproate is avoided in people who can become pregnant. Lithium may be continued with specialist care, fetal echocardiography and close level monitoring, because clearance rises in pregnancy and falls abruptly after delivery.
Exam trap: a stable patient on lithium who starts hydrochlorothiazide or ibuprofen and becomes tremulous and confused has lithium toxicity until proved otherwise.
High-yield: lithium-induced polyuria with dilute urine that does not concentrate after desmopressin is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; amiloride reduces lithium entry into principal cells.

s23e-s11a01.bodyHtml:
This group of disorders shares one feature: bodily symptoms, or worry about illness, cause distress and impairment out of proportion to any medical finding. The symptoms are not intentionally produced, which separates the whole group from factitious disorder and malingering.

The four main diagnoses

DisorderCore featureKey point
Somatic symptom disorderOne or more distressing bodily symptoms plus excessive thoughts, worry or time spent on them, usually for 6 months or moreThe symptoms do not have to be medically unexplained; a real disease with a disproportionate response still qualifies
Illness anxiety disorderPreoccupation with having or getting a serious illness; bodily symptoms absent or mildRepeated checking and reassurance-seeking, or avoidance of doctors altogether
Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder)Motor or sensory symptoms (weakness, abnormal movements, non-epileptic attacks, sensory or visual loss) that are inconsistent with recognised neurological diseaseDiagnosed by positive clinical signs; a recent stressor is common but no longer required
Psychological factors affecting other medical conditionsA known medical condition is made worse by behaviour or emotion (denial, nonadherence, anxiety triggering attacks)The medical disease is the primary problem

The decision tree below separates these disorders from the conditions in which symptoms are produced on purpose.

Positive signs of functional weakness and sensory loss

  • Hoover sign: hip extension on the weak side is weak when tested directly but becomes strong when the patient flexes the opposite hip against resistance, an automatic movement.
  • Hip abductor sign: the same principle, using hip abduction.
  • Dragging gait with the leg pulled behind like a dead weight, rather than circumducted.
  • Tubular visual field: the field stays the same width whether tested at 1 metre or at 2 metres, which is optically impossible.
  • Functional tremor that changes frequency to match a rhythm tapped by the other hand (entrainment) and stops with distraction.

Non-epileptic attacks versus epileptic seizures

FeatureFavours functional (non-epileptic) attackFavours epileptic seizure
EyesClosed, resisting openingOpen
MovementsSide-to-side head shaking, out-of-phase limb movements, pelvic thrusting, waxing and waningSynchronous, stereotyped from one event to the next
Duration and recoveryOften longer than 2 minutes; rapid recovery, sometimes with cryingUsually under 2 minutes; postictal confusion
OtherRecall of the eventTongue bitten on its side; events arising from sleep

Video-EEG that records a typical event, with no epileptiform activity, establishes the diagnosis.

Exam trap: a patient with confirmed rheumatoid arthritis who spends hours a day researching her pain and visits the emergency department weekly can still have somatic symptom disorder. Ask about the response to the symptom, not only whether a disease explains it.
High-yield: two questions sort most vignettes. Are the symptoms produced on purpose? If yes, is there an obvious external reward? No and no points to a somatic symptom disorder; yes and no to factitious disorder; yes and yes to malingering.

s23e-s11a02.bodyHtml:
In factitious disorder imposed on self, a person falsifies symptoms or deliberately causes illness or injury in themselves and presents as ill, without an obvious external reward. The motive is psychological, usually the care and attention of the sick role. In factitious disorder imposed on another, a caregiver does the same to a dependent, most often a parent to a young child; the diagnosis belongs to the caregiver, and the child is a victim of abuse. Malingering is deliberate feigning for an external goal such as money, drugs, time off work or avoiding prosecution. It is a behaviour, not a mental disorder.

Somatic symptom disordersFactitious disorderMalingering
Symptoms produced on purposeNoYesYes
MotiveNot consciousInternal: to be seen as illExternal: an identifiable reward
Response to the end of the rewardPersistsOften moves on to another hospitalSymptoms fade once the goal is reached or lost

Laboratory clues to self-induced illness

Many factitious presentations rest on a drug the patient can obtain, often through health care work. The physiology of each hormone or drug explains the pattern.

PresentationPatternWhy
Hypoglycemia from injected insulinHigh insulin, low C-peptideBeta cells cleave proinsulin into insulin and C-peptide in equal amounts; injected insulin carries no C-peptide and suppresses the patient's own secretion
Hypoglycemia from a sulfonylureaHigh insulin, high C-peptide, positive drug screenThe drug closes beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channels, so the patient's own beta cells secrete; only the screen separates this from an insulinoma
Thyrotoxicosis from thyroid hormone tabletsLow TSH, high free T4, low radioiodine uptake, low thyroglobulinThe gland is suppressed and releases little thyroglobulin, whereas thyroiditis releases it from damaged follicles
Bleeding from warfarin or a long-acting rodenticide anticoagulantProlonged PT and INR that correct on mixing; low factors II, VII, IX and XVitamin K epoxide reductase is blocked, so the vitamin K-dependent factors are not activated
Recurrent infections or woundsMixed skin or gut organisms in blood; wounds only where the hands can reachInjection of contaminated material, or self-inflicted injury
Exam trap: a high insulin with a high C-peptide is not proof of an insulinoma. Screen for sulfonylureas and meglitinides before imaging the pancreas.
High-yield: people with factitious disorder are often eager for invasive tests and surgery, give a dramatic but inconsistent history, and have records at several hospitals. Many work in health care.

s23e-s11a03.bodyHtml:
The three main eating disorders

Anorexia nervosaBulimia nervosaBinge-eating disorder
WeightSignificantly lowUsually normal or aboveOften obesity
Core behaviourRestriction, sometimes with bingeing and purging (binge-eating/purging type)Binges with compensatory purging, fasting or exercise, at least weekly for 3 monthsBinges with distress, at least weekly for 3 months, without regular compensation
Body imageIntense fear of weight gain; distorted view of own bodySelf-worth tied to shape and weightNot required

Amenorrhea is common in anorexia nervosa but is no longer a diagnostic criterion.

Starvation physiology in anorexia nervosa

  • Fuel: after the first days of fasting the brain shifts largely to ketone bodies, which spares muscle protein from being burned for gluconeogenesis.
  • Reproductive axis: low leptin and energy deficit slow hypothalamic GnRH pulses, so LH, FSH and estradiol are all low (hypothalamic amenorrhea). Low estrogen, together with high cortisol and low IGF-1, causes bone loss.
  • Thyroid: peripheral conversion shifts from T3 to reverse T3, so T3 is low with a normal or low TSH; this is an adaptation, not hypothyroidism, and is not treated.
  • Growth hormone is raised but IGF-1 is low (hepatic resistance).
  • Other findings: bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, lanugo hair, yellowish skin from high carotene, leukopenia, and delayed gastric emptying.

Acid-base clues to purging

BehaviourBloodUrine chloride
Self-induced vomitingHypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosisLow (chloride is conserved)
Diuretic misuseHypokalemic metabolic alkalosisHigh while the drug is acting
Laxative misuseHypokalemia; often a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis from stool bicarbonate lossVariable

Vomiting removes hydrochloric acid, so bicarbonate rises. The volume loss stimulates aldosterone, which drives potassium and hydrogen ion secretion in the collecting duct and keeps the alkalosis going. Parotid swelling raises the serum amylase (salivary type), and gastric acid erodes the inner surfaces of the upper front teeth.

Refeeding: why phosphate falls

Feeding after starvation releases insulin. Insulin moves glucose into cells, where glycolysis and ATP production consume phosphate, and it shifts potassium and magnesium inward too. Total-body stores are already depleted, so serum phosphate can fall steeply within the first days. Low phosphate means low ATP and low red-cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, with muscle and diaphragm weakness, heart failure, arrhythmias, hemolysis, rhabdomyolysis, seizures and delirium. A carbohydrate load can also use up the remaining thiamine.

Drugs by mechanism

  • Fluoxetine (serotonin reuptake inhibitor) reduces binge and purge frequency in bulimia nervosa.
  • Bupropion (norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibitor) is contraindicated in bulimia and anorexia nervosa because it lowers the seizure threshold, and the electrolyte disturbances add to the risk.
  • Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug converted to dextroamphetamine, which releases dopamine and norepinephrine; it is approved for moderate to severe binge-eating disorder in adults.
Exam trap: a low T3 in a starving patient is not hypothyroidism. Thyroid hormone replacement is wrong; weight restoration corrects it.
