s23e-s11a04.bodyHtml:
Pica

Pica is persistent eating of non-food substances (soil, clay, paint chips, ice, paper) for at least 1 month at an age when this is developmentally inappropriate, usually after age 2. It is common in iron deficiency, pregnancy, intellectual disability and autism.

  • Ice craving (pagophagia) is closely tied to iron deficiency and usually stops with iron replacement.
  • Paint chips in an older home raise the concern of lead poisoning. Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, so heme synthesis fails: microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling, abdominal pain, and neurodevelopmental harm in children.
  • Other complications are bowel obstruction from bezoars and parasite infection from soil.

Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID)

Eating is restricted because of sensory aversion to texture, smell or taste, lack of interest in food, or fear of choking or vomiting. The result is weight loss, failure to grow, nutritional deficiency, dependence on supplements or social impairment. Unlike anorexia nervosa there is no fear of weight gain and no body-image disturbance. It often begins in childhood and is common in autism.

Impulse-control disorders

DisorderPatternDistinguish from
Intermittent explosive disorderRecurrent, unplanned outbursts of verbal or physical aggression grossly out of proportion to the trigger, followed by regret; age 6 or olderAntisocial personality (planned, for gain), mania, borderline personality
KleptomaniaRepeated failure to resist stealing objects not needed for use or for their value; tension before and relief during the actOrdinary theft (for gain), mania, conduct disorder
PyromaniaDeliberate fire-setting on more than one occasion, with arousal beforehand and fascination with fire, not for money, revenge or ideologyConduct disorder, arson for gain
Gambling disorderPersistent problem gambling with chasing of losses, lying and escalating stakes; classified with the addictive disordersGambling during a manic episode

Drug-induced impulse control

Dopamine agonists such as pramipexole and ropinirole stimulate D2 and D3 receptors, including those in the mesolimbic reward pathway. They can cause compulsive gambling, shopping, eating or sexual behaviour in patients with Parkinson disease or restless legs syndrome. Patients often hide it, so ask directly.

High-yield: naltrexone, a mu-opioid receptor antagonist, dampens the reward of the behaviour and has some evidence in kleptomania and gambling disorder.

s23e-s11b01.bodyHtml:
Patients with somatic symptom disorders are common in primary care and emergency medicine. They are not choosing their symptoms, and they deserve the same respect as any other patient.

Diagnosis

  • Take the symptoms seriously and do an appropriate assessment once. Look for red flags that need further testing, such as weight loss, fever, objective neurological signs or abnormal laboratory results.
  • Make the diagnosis on positive grounds: the disproportionate thoughts and behaviours in somatic symptom disorder, the health anxiety in illness anxiety disorder, and the positive neurological signs in functional neurological symptom disorder.
  • Screen for depression, anxiety, substance use and suicidal thinking, which often coexist.
  • In suspected non-epileptic attacks, video-EEG monitoring that records a typical event is the diagnostic test.

Management of somatic symptom disorder and illness anxiety disorder

  • One primary care physician coordinates all care.
  • Regularly scheduled, brief visits (for example every 4 to 6 weeks) instead of visits on demand, with a focused examination each time.
  • Avoid tests, referrals and procedures that are not clinically indicated; each normal result gives only short relief.
  • Set goals around function (work, sleep, activity) rather than cure.
  • Cognitive behavioural therapy has the best evidence. An SSRI or SNRI helps when depression or anxiety coexists.
  • Avoid escalating opioids and benzodiazepines.

Management of functional neurological symptom disorder

  • Explain the diagnosis clearly. Show the patient the positive signs, for example the Hoover sign, and explain that the nervous system is not damaged but is not working properly. Say that the condition is real, common and can improve.
  • Refer for specialist physiotherapy for functional weakness and gait disorders, and for psychological therapy (CBT-based) for non-epileptic attacks.
  • Taper antiseizure drugs that were started for non-epileptic attacks alone, under neurology supervision, once the diagnosis is secure.
  • A better outcome is linked to short duration, acute onset and early diagnosis that the patient accepts. Long duration and ongoing disability claims predict a poorer outcome.

Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions

Here a medical illness is real and is worsened by behaviour or emotion: for example, a man whose fear of bad news delays assessment of chest pain, or an adolescent who omits insulin because of anxiety. Treat the medical illness and address the psychological factor directly.

Exam trap: "There is nothing wrong with you" and "it is all stress" are the wrong things to say. The right answer acknowledges the symptoms, names the diagnosis and offers a plan.
High-yield: an objective sign of neurological disease (an extensor plantar response, a fixed field defect, muscle wasting) does not fit a functional diagnosis and needs investigation.

s23e-s11b02.bodyHtml:
Recognising factitious disorder imposed on self

  • A dramatic but inconsistent history, symptoms that appear only when unobserved, and failure to respond to standard treatment.
  • Eagerness for invasive tests and operations, many hospital records, and new symptoms when tests come back normal.
  • Specific tests can expose deception: supervised temperature measurement for factitious fever, C-peptide and drug screens for hypoglycemia, thyroglobulin for thyrotoxicosis, stool laxative screens for chronic diarrhea, and drug levels for unexplained bleeding.

Management

  • Involve psychiatry early, and keep the team's approach consistent.
  • Discuss the findings with the patient in a supportive, nonpunitive way. Express concern, and offer continued care and psychological treatment. An angry confrontation usually makes the patient leave and present elsewhere.
  • Avoid unnecessary procedures, and have one physician coordinate care.
  • For long-acting rodenticide anticoagulants, bleeding is reversed with intravenous vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate. High-dose oral vitamin K is then continued for weeks to months, with INR checks, because the poison persists.

Factitious disorder imposed on another

Suspect it when a child has repeated, unexplained illness that occurs only with one caregiver present, unusual organisms or drugs in samples, or symptoms nobody else has witnessed, and that improves when the child is separated from that caregiver. It is child maltreatment: protect the child and report to child protective services. The physician does not need proof before reporting; reasonable suspicion is enough.

Malingering

Look for a clear external incentive: a pending lawsuit or disability claim, a request for opioids or benzodiazepines, avoidance of work or military duty, or a court date. Symptoms are vague or exaggerated, the patient is reluctant to cooperate with assessment, and the complaints fade once the goal is reached. Document the objective findings and discuss the inconsistencies with the patient calmly. Do not give the drug or certificate that is not indicated.

Exam trap: in a child, the next step after recognising possible factitious illness is a report to child protective services, not confrontation of the parent or more tests on the child.

s23e-s11b03.bodyHtml:
Assessment

  • Weight, height and BMI (BMI percentile or percent of median BMI in children and adolescents), heart rate and blood pressure lying and standing, and temperature.
  • Electrolytes, including phosphate and magnesium, glucose, kidney and liver function, a blood count and an ECG (bradycardia, QT prolongation).
  • Ask about purging, laxatives, diuretics, exercise, suicidal thoughts and substance use.

When to admit

Admit for medical stabilisation when there is instability. Examples are marked bradycardia (in adolescents, a daytime heart rate below 50/min), hypotension or marked orthostatic change, hypothermia, electrolyte disturbance, arrhythmia or a prolonged QT interval, or syncope. Very low weight (for example below 75% of median BMI in adolescents), acute food refusal, failed outpatient treatment and suicidality are further reasons. Thresholds differ between adults and adolescents.

Refeeding syndrome: prevent, then watch

Risk is highest with very low BMI, rapid recent weight loss, little or no intake for more than about 10 days, or low potassium, phosphate or magnesium before feeding.

  • Check electrolytes before feeding and give thiamine before carbohydrate.
  • Start nutrition and advance it steadily under monitoring; correct low levels as they appear.
  • Check phosphate, potassium, magnesium and glucose daily for the first several days, and watch for edema, heart failure and arrhythmia.

Treatment

DisorderFirst lineMedication
Anorexia nervosaNutritional rehabilitation with weight restoration and psychotherapy; family-based treatment for adolescentsNo drug reliably restores weight; treat coexisting depression or anxiety as needed
Bulimia nervosaCognitive behavioural therapy for eating disordersFluoxetine, at a higher dose than for depression (60 mg daily); never bupropion
Binge-eating disorderCognitive behavioural therapyLisdexamfetamine (approved in adults) or an SSRI

Complications to know

  • Bone loss in anorexia nervosa: weight restoration with return of menses is the main treatment. Combined oral contraceptives do not protect bone and can mask recovery of menses.
  • Purging: hypokalemia with arrhythmia, dental erosion, parotid swelling, esophagitis, and rarely esophageal rupture.
  • Binge-eating disorder: obesity, type 2 diabetes and the metabolic syndrome.
Exam trap: weight restoration, not an antidepressant, is the treatment for depressed mood and obsessional thinking in a starving patient; both often improve with refeeding.

s23e-s11b04.bodyHtml:
Pica

  • Check a blood count and ferritin, and replace iron when it is low. Ice craving in pregnancy or heavy menstrual bleeding is a common clue.
  • In a young child who eats paint chips or soil, measure a venous blood lead level and look at the home for sources of lead.
  • Treat with behavioural approaches, supervision and removal of the substances; look for intellectual disability or autism.

ARFID

  • Assess growth, nutrition and complications as you would in anorexia nervosa; severe cases also need medical stabilisation.
  • Rule out medical causes of poor intake (celiac disease, eosinophilic esophagitis, swallowing problems).
  • Treatment is graded exposure to feared or new foods within cognitive behavioural therapy, with a dietitian and family involvement.

Impulse-control disorders

DisorderTreatment
Intermittent explosive disorderCognitive behavioural therapy (relaxation, recognising triggers); an SSRI such as fluoxetine has some evidence
KleptomaniaCognitive behavioural therapy; naltrexone has some evidence
PyromaniaPsychotherapy; assess for conduct disorder and risk to others
Gambling disorderCognitive behavioural therapy and peer support groups; naltrexone has some evidence; address debt and suicide risk

Ask about dopamine agonists

A patient with Parkinson disease or restless legs syndrome who starts gambling, shopping or eating compulsively should have the dopamine agonist reduced or stopped gradually. Stopping abruptly risks a withdrawal syndrome of anxiety, low mood and pain.

High-yield: before diagnosing intermittent explosive disorder, rule out mania, substance intoxication, a head injury and a personality disorder with planned aggression.

s23e-s12a01.bodyHtml:
Neurodevelopmental disorders begin in the developmental period, often before school entry, and impair personal, social, academic or occupational functioning. Several cluster together: a child with one has a high chance of another.

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)

  • Core features: a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, present in two or more settings (for example, home and school), with several symptoms present before age 12 and lasting at least 6 months.
  • Neurobiology: heritability is high (twin estimates around 70–80%). Imaging shows delayed cortical maturation and altered fronto-striatal circuits, where dopamine and noradrenaline tune attention and inhibition.
  • Course: hyperactivity tends to fade in adolescence; inattention more often persists into adulthood.
DrugMechanismNotable adverse effects
MethylphenidateBlocks the dopamine and noradrenaline transporters (reuptake inhibition)Reduced appetite, insomnia, raised heart rate and blood pressure, slowed growth velocity
AmphetaminesEnter the terminal, reverse the transporters and displace monoamines from vesicles (release)As for methylphenidate; higher misuse potential
Atomoxetine, viloxazineSelective noradrenaline reuptake inhibition (nonstimulants)Suicidal thinking in young people (boxed warning for atomoxetine), rare liver injury
Guanfacine, clonidine (extended release)Alpha-2 adrenergic agonistsSedation, hypotension, bradycardia; rebound hypertension if stopped abruptly

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)

ASD combines persistent deficits in social communication and interaction (reciprocity, nonverbal communication, relationships) with restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities, including insistence on sameness and unusual sensory responses. Signs appear in early childhood. It is about four times more common in boys. Intellectual ability ranges from impaired to superior, and language may be absent, delayed or fluent.

Genetic contributors include fragile X syndrome (FMR1 CGG-repeat expansion), tuberous sclerosis, copy-number variants found on chromosomal microarray, and many single-gene variants. Vaccines do not cause autism.

Intellectual disability

Deficits in intellectual functioning (reasoning, problem solving, learning; usually an IQ about two standard deviations below the mean, near 70 or lower) together with deficits in adaptive functioning (conceptual, social and practical). Severity is graded by adaptive function, not by IQ alone.

  • Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is the most common genetic cause.
  • Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause: long face, large ears, large testes after puberty, hyperextensible joints, often with autistic features.
  • Other causes: fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (the most common preventable cause), congenital hypothyroidism and untreated phenylketonuria (both prevented by newborn screening), congenital infections, and perinatal hypoxia.

Tic disorders and Tourette disorder

Tics are sudden, rapid, recurrent, nonrhythmic movements or vocalisations, often preceded by an urge and briefly suppressible. Tourette disorder needs multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, beginning before age 18 and present for more than a year. Tics usually peak around age 10–12 and lessen by adulthood. ADHD and obsessive-compulsive disorder commonly co-occur; dopamine pathways in the basal ganglia are implicated, which is why dopamine-blocking drugs suppress tics.

Specific learning disorder

Persistent difficulty in reading (dyslexia), written expression or mathematics, well below what is expected for age despite adequate intelligence, instruction and sensory function. Dyslexia reflects a phonological processing deficit.

High-yield: a child whose hyperactivity appears only at school, or only at home, does not meet the setting requirement for ADHD. Look instead for a setting-specific stressor, a learning disorder or an anxiety disorder.
Exam trap: a child with autism and an IQ in the normal range still has autism. Language and intelligence are specifiers, not diagnostic criteria.

s23e-s12a02.bodyHtml:
Several childhood diagnoses describe anger, rule-breaking or irritability. They are separated by what the behaviour targets, how severe it is and the age limits written into the criteria.

DisorderCore pictureKey age rule
Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD)Angry or irritable mood, arguing with and defying authority figures, spitefulness; no serious violation of others' rightsLasts at least 6 months
Conduct disorderViolates the basic rights of others or major social rules: aggression to people or animals, destroying property, deceit or theft, serious rule-breaking such as truancy or running awayChildhood-onset type if a symptom appears before 10
Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (DMDD)Severe temper outbursts about three or more times a week, with persistently irritable or angry mood between them, for at least a yearOnset before 10; first diagnosed only between ages 6 and 18
Antisocial personality disorderAdult pattern of disregard for others' rightsAge 18 or older, with conduct disorder that began before 15

DMDD was introduced partly to avoid labelling chronically irritable children with bipolar disorder: it predicts later depression and anxiety, not mania. When a child meets criteria for both DMDD and ODD, only DMDD is diagnosed.

Elimination disorders

  • Enuresis: repeated voiding into bed or clothes at least twice a week for 3 months (or with marked distress), at a developmental age of at least 5. Most cases are primary and nocturnal, with a strong family history; delayed maturation of arousal to bladder signals and nighttime vasopressin release both contribute. Secondary enuresis (after at least 6 months dry) raises concern for urinary infection, diabetes mellitus or insipidus, constipation, sleep apnoea or psychosocial stress.
  • Encopresis: repeated passage of stool in inappropriate places at a developmental age of at least 4. Most children have chronic constipation with liquid stool leaking around retained faeces (overflow).

Disorders after severe neglect

Children who have lacked consistent caregivers (institutional care, repeated changes of foster carer) can develop one of two patterns:

  • Reactive attachment disorder: emotionally withdrawn and inhibited; rarely seeks or responds to comfort when distressed.
  • Disinhibited social engagement disorder: overly familiar with strangers, wanders off without checking back with the caregiver.

Selective mutism

A child who speaks normally at home consistently fails to speak in specific social settings such as school, for at least a month (not counting the first month of school). It is closely tied to social anxiety rather than to a language disorder.

High-yield: the anger in ODD is aimed at authority figures; conduct disorder harms other people, animals or property. The age-15 link to antisocial personality disorder is a favourite exam fact.

s23e-s12a03.bodyHtml:
A personality disorder is an enduring, inflexible and pervasive pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates from cultural expectations, begins by adolescence or early adulthood, is stable over time and causes distress or impairment. The traits usually feel natural to the person (ego-syntonic), so they rarely seek help for the traits themselves; they present with the consequences.

Cluster A: odd or eccentric

  • Paranoid: pervasive distrust; reads hidden threats into benign remarks; bears grudges. Main defence: projection.
  • Schizoid: detached, prefers solitary activities, little interest in relationships or sex, emotionally flat. No odd beliefs.
  • Schizotypal: odd beliefs or magical thinking, ideas of reference (not fixed delusions), unusual perceptions, odd speech and appearance, social anxiety that does not fade with familiarity. It is genetically linked to schizophrenia and can precede it.

Cluster B: dramatic, emotional or erratic

  • Antisocial: disregard for and violation of others' rights, deceit, impulsivity, irritability and aggression, recklessness, lack of remorse. Needs age at least 18 and conduct disorder before 15. Much more common in men.
  • Borderline: unstable relationships and self-image, frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, impulsivity, recurrent suicidal behaviour or self-harm, intense mood reactivity, chronic emptiness, intense anger, and transient stress-related paranoia or dissociation. Typical defences: splitting (people are all good or all bad) and projective identification. Childhood trauma and invalidating environments are risk factors.
  • Histrionic: attention-seeking, seductive or provocative behaviour, shallow and rapidly shifting emotion, impressionistic speech, uses appearance to draw attention.
  • Narcissistic: grandiosity, need for admiration, sense of entitlement, lack of empathy; fragile self-esteem beneath, so criticism provokes rage or humiliation.

Cluster C: anxious or fearful

  • Avoidant: wants relationships but avoids them for fear of criticism or rejection; feels inadequate.
  • Dependent: needs others to take responsibility and make everyday decisions; cannot disagree for fear of losing support; quickly seeks a new relationship when one ends.
  • Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD): preoccupation with order, rules and perfection that defeats the purpose of the task; rigid, stubborn, reluctant to delegate.

Look-alikes

PairHow to tell them apart
Schizoid vs schizotypalSchizoid people are detached but not odd; schizotypal people have eccentric beliefs and perceptions
Schizotypal vs schizophreniaSchizophrenia has frank psychosis (fixed delusions, persistent hallucinations) for a month or more
Schizoid vs avoidantSchizoid people do not want relationships; avoidant people do but are afraid
OCPD vs OCDOCPD traits are ego-syntonic, with no true obsessions or compulsions; OCD symptoms are intrusive and unwanted (ego-dystonic)
Borderline vs bipolar disorderBorderline mood shifts last hours and follow interpersonal triggers; bipolar episodes last days to weeks
Exam trap: a personality disorder should not be diagnosed from behaviour that appears only during a mood episode, intoxication or a new medical illness. The pattern must be long-standing.

s23e-s12b01.bodyHtml:
ADHD

Diagnosis is clinical. Collect standardised rating scales from parents and teachers to confirm symptoms in more than one setting, and screen for look-alikes and comorbidity: hearing or vision problems, learning disorders, anxiety, depression, sleep problems (including sleep apnoea), absence seizures, substance use in adolescents, and adversity or abuse. Laboratory tests, EEG and imaging are not part of routine evaluation.

AgeFirst-line approach
Preschool (4–5 years)Parent training in behaviour management and classroom behavioural support first; add methylphenidate only if improvement is inadequate and impairment is moderate to severe
School age (6–11 years)A stimulant medication together with behavioural therapy and school supports
Adolescents (12–18 years)A stimulant, with the adolescent's agreement, plus behavioural and school interventions; watch for diversion of stimulants
  • Before a stimulant: ask about fainting with exercise, palpitations, chest pain and sudden cardiac death in young relatives, and examine the heart. A routine ECG is not needed without such findings.
  • Monitoring: height, weight, heart rate and blood pressure. Appetite loss and insomnia are the commonest problems; give the dose with or after breakfast and avoid late doses.
  • Nonstimulants (atomoxetine, viloxazine, extended-release guanfacine or clonidine) are used when stimulants fail or are not tolerated, when there is concern about misuse, or, for alpha-2 agonists, when tics or sleep problems coexist.

Autism spectrum disorder

  • Screen all toddlers with a validated autism tool at the 18- and 24-month visits, in addition to general developmental surveillance.
  • Red flags at any age: no babbling or pointing by 12 months, no single words by 16 months, no spontaneous two-word phrases by 24 months, and any loss of language or social skills.
  • When screening is positive: refer at the same time for a diagnostic evaluation and for early intervention services; do not wait for the diagnosis to start therapy. Arrange a formal hearing test.
  • Genetic testing is offered to every child diagnosed with ASD: chromosomal microarray and fragile X testing (more targeted tests if the examination suggests a syndrome).
  • Treatment: intensive behavioural intervention (such as applied behaviour analysis), speech-language and occupational therapy, and educational supports. Medication treats associated symptoms only: risperidone and aripiprazole for severe irritability and aggression (monitor weight, glucose and lipids), and ADHD medicines for co-occurring ADHD.

Tics and Tourette disorder

Explain the usual course (waxing and waning, improvement in adolescence) and treat only if tics cause pain, social harm or impairment. Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics (habit reversal) is first-line. Medication options: alpha-2 agonists (guanfacine, clonidine), especially with ADHD; antipsychotics (aripiprazole, risperidone, haloperidol) for severe tics, at the cost of metabolic or movement side effects. Look for co-occurring ADHD and obsessive-compulsive disorder, which often cause more impairment than the tics.

Exam trap: a child with a positive autism screen and parents worried about speech should be referred for early intervention immediately, not after "watchful waiting" or a repeat screen in 6 months.

Look for co-occurring ADHD and obsessive-compulsive disorder, which often cause more impairment than the tics.
a child with a positive autism screen and parents worried about speech should be referred for early intervention immediately, not after "watchful waiting" or a repeat screen in 6 months.

s23e-s12b02.bodyHtml:
Oppositional defiant disorder and conduct disorder

  • First-line treatment is psychosocial: parent management training (consistent limits, praise and rewards for wanted behaviour, predictable consequences), plus school-based and, for older children and teens, multisystemic or family therapy.
  • Treat comorbid ADHD, which is common and worsens outcomes; stimulants often reduce aggression too.
  • Antipsychotics are reserved for severe, persistent aggression that has not responded to psychosocial treatment.
  • Always ask about abuse, bullying, substance use and learning problems. In conduct disorder, assess for safety risks to others and the legal context.

Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder

Parent training and psychotherapy (cognitive behavioural approaches to irritability) come first; stimulants help when ADHD coexists, and SSRIs are sometimes used for the irritability. Mood stabilisers for bipolar disorder are not indicated, because DMDD is not a bipolar condition.

Nocturnal enuresis

  • Evaluate: history (daytime symptoms, constipation, snoring, thirst, stressors), examination of the abdomen, back and genitals, and a urinalysis (glucose, specific gravity, infection).
  • Before age 5 it is developmentally normal and needs only reassurance. Many children outgrow it each year without treatment.
  • Behavioural measures: void before bed, limit evening fluids, avoid caffeine, never punish.
  • Enuresis alarm: the most effective long-term treatment with the lowest relapse rate, but it needs weeks of family commitment.
  • Desmopressin: works quickly (useful for sleepovers or camp) but relapse after stopping is common. Restrict fluids from an hour before the dose until morning because of the risk of water intoxication and hyponatraemia.
  • Treat constipation first if present; it often resolves the wetting.

Encopresis

Most children with soiling have retentive constipation. Treatment: education that removes blame, disimpaction (oral polyethylene glycol at high dose, or enemas), then maintenance stool softener for months with scheduled toilet sitting after meals and a reward chart. Consider abuse if soiling begins suddenly with behaviour change.

Selective mutism

Treat as an anxiety disorder: cognitive behavioural therapy with graded exposure, involving school staff; an SSRI may be added for severe or persistent cases. Check hearing and language development first.

After severe neglect

For reactive attachment disorder the core treatment is a stable, nurturing caregiver, supported by caregiver-focused therapy. Report suspected ongoing neglect or abuse to child protective services.

High-yield: a previously dry 7-year-old who starts wetting again needs a urinalysis and a search for a medical or psychosocial cause, not an alarm.

s23e-s12b03.bodyHtml:
Psychotherapy is the main treatment for every personality disorder. Medication treats co-occurring conditions (depression, anxiety disorders, substance use) or specific target symptoms for short periods; no drug is approved for a personality disorder itself.

Borderline personality disorder

  • Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) has the strongest evidence for reducing self-harm and suicide attempts. It teaches distress tolerance, emotion regulation, mindfulness and interpersonal skills. Mentalisation-based therapy and other structured therapies are alternatives.
  • Assess suicide risk at every visit: lifetime risk of death by suicide is substantially raised.
  • Avoid benzodiazepines (disinhibition, misuse) and be cautious with drugs that are dangerous in overdose; prescribe limited quantities.
  • Many patients improve markedly over years; symptom remission is common by middle age.

Other disorders

  • Antisocial: treat substance use and other comorbidity; structured programmes can reduce reoffending, but engagement is often poor.
  • Schizotypal: supportive and social-skills therapy; low-dose antipsychotics for brief psychotic-like periods.
  • Avoidant: cognitive behavioural therapy with graded exposure, as for social anxiety, with which it overlaps; SSRIs help when social anxiety disorder coexists.
  • Dependent, OCPD, narcissistic, histrionic: individual psychotherapy.

Working with patients who have personality disorders

PatternHelpful approach
Borderline: idealises then devalues staff, splits the team, frequent unscheduled callsOne consistent clinician or plan, clear and predictable boundaries, regularly scheduled visits, team meetings so all staff give the same message; stay calm and nonjudgmental
Narcissistic: demands the "best" doctor, dismisses othersAcknowledge the patient's concerns and expertise without confrontation; frame recommendations in terms of the patient's own goals
Paranoid: suspicious of motivesExplain each step clearly and honestly, be straightforward and avoid overly friendly behaviour
Histrionic: flirtatious or dramaticMaintain professional boundaries, use a chaperone where appropriate, focus on objective findings
Dependent: frequent calls, cannot decideRegularly scheduled visits, reassurance with firm limits, encourage self-reliance
Obsessive-compulsive personality: wants every detailGive thorough, precise information and involve the patient in planning
Exam trap: when a patient with borderline traits praises you and criticises a colleague, do not agree or defend the colleague's character; acknowledge the patient's feelings, restate the shared care plan and keep the team aligned.

s23e-s13a01.bodyHtml:
Grief is the expected response to the death of someone close. It comes in waves, often set off by reminders, and the person can still feel pleasure and keeps a sense of self-worth. Briefly hearing or seeing the dead person, especially when falling asleep, is common and is not psychosis. Most people find that the intensity eases over months while the loss stays part of life.

Telling grief from its disorders

FeatureOrdinary griefProlonged grief disorderMajor depressive episode
Time since the deathAnyAt least 12 months in adults (6 months in children and adolescents)Any; bereavement does not rule it out
Core experienceWaves of sadness tied to remindersPersistent yearning for, or preoccupation with, the dead person nearly every dayPervasive low mood or loss of pleasure in almost everything
Self-imagePreservedFeels part of self has died; identity disruptedWorthlessness, guilt beyond the loss
Other featuresFunction returns graduallyAvoidance of reminders, disbelief, numbness, life feels meaningless, intense lonelinessPsychomotor change, sleep and appetite change, suicidal thoughts

Prolonged grief disorder also needs clinically significant distress or impairment and a reaction that clearly exceeds the person's cultural and religious norms.

Suicide: who is at risk

  • The strongest single predictor of death by suicide is a previous suicide attempt.
  • Women make more attempts; men die by suicide more often, largely because they use more lethal methods.
  • In the United States, firearms account for about half of suicide deaths, so access to a gun greatly raises the chance that an attempt is fatal.
  • Other risk factors: psychiatric illness (depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, substance use), hopelessness, older age in men, living alone, recent loss or discharge from a psychiatric unit, chronic pain or serious illness, and a family history of suicide.
  • Protective factors: social connection, children at home, reasons for living, religious or cultural beliefs against suicide, and access to care.

Nonsuicidal self-injury

Deliberate damage to one's own body, such as cutting or burning the skin, without the intent to die. It usually starts in adolescence. People describe quick relief from tension or emotional pain. In learning-theory terms, the removal of an unpleasant state makes the behaviour more likely: negative reinforcement. Self-injury is not a suicide attempt, but it raises the long-term risk of suicide and always deserves a suicide risk assessment.

Exam trap: asking directly about suicidal thoughts does not plant the idea or raise risk. Not asking is the error.
High-yield: in learning theory, reinforcement (positive or negative) always increases a behaviour, and punishment always decreases it. "Negative" means something is taken away.

s23e-s13a02.bodyHtml:
Intimate partner violence

Physical, sexual or psychological harm, or controlling behaviour, by a current or former partner. Clues include injuries that do not match the story, delay in seeking care, injuries in different stages of healing, injuries during pregnancy, frequent visits with vague complaints, and a partner who will not leave the room or answers for the patient. Risk of serious harm rises when the victim tries to leave, and with threats involving weapons or attempted strangulation.

Elder abuse and neglect

FormWhat it looks like
PhysicalUnexplained bruises (for example, grip marks on the upper arms), fractures, burns
PsychologicalThreats, humiliation, isolation from friends and family
Financial exploitationMoney or property taken or misused; sudden changes to a will or bank accounts
Caregiver neglectA responsible caregiver fails to provide food, hygiene, medicines or care: weight loss, pressure injuries, soiled clothing
Self-neglectAn older adult living alone who cannot or does not meet their own basic needs
SexualAny non-consensual sexual contact

The abuser is most often someone the person depends on, usually a family member. Cognitive impairment, dependence for daily care and social isolation raise the risk.

Delirium, dementia and depression in older adults

FeatureDeliriumDementiaDepression
OnsetHours to daysMonths to yearsWeeks to months
Attention and awarenessImpaired and fluctuatingUsually intact until lateEffortful, poor concentration
CourseWorse at night; usually reversible if the cause is treatedSlowly progressiveImproves with treatment
Testing behaviourDistractible, cannot sustain a taskTries, may confabulate"I don't know" answers, low effort
EEGDiffuse slowing (fast activity in sedative withdrawal)Normal early, slowing lateNormal

Changing health behaviour

The stages-of-change model describes readiness, not a fixed sequence: people move back and forth, and relapse is expected rather than a failure. Matching the conversation to the stage is more effective than pushing for action that the person is not ready for.

Motivational interviewing is a collaborative, non-confrontational style that helps a person find their own reasons to change. Its tools are open questions, affirmations, reflections and summaries. A double-sided reflection states both sides of the person's ambivalence back to them. The clinician avoids arguing, lecturing and labelling, and draws out "change talk" from the patient.

Exam trap: in delirium the defining problem is attention and level of awareness. Memory loss alone does not separate delirium from dementia.

s23e-s13a03.bodyHtml:
Autonomic control of the male sexual response

PhaseMain pathwayMechanism
ErectionParasympathetic: pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4) via the cavernous nervesNitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase; cGMP relaxes cavernosal smooth muscle and blood fills the sinusoids
EmissionSympathetic: hypogastric nerves (T11 to L2)Contraction of the vas deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate; the internal urethral sphincter closes
Expulsion (ejaculation)Somatic: pudendal nerveRhythmic contraction of the bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus

The cavernous nerves run along the posterolateral prostate, so radical prostatectomy and pelvic surgery or radiation commonly cause erectile dysfunction.

PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) block the breakdown of cGMP, so they amplify the nitric oxide signal; they need sexual stimulation to work. Nitrates also raise cGMP, and the combination can cause profound hypotension. Adverse effects: headache, flushing, nasal congestion, and blue-tinged vision with sildenafil (it also inhibits PDE6 in the retina).

Drugs that impair sexual function

Drug groupTypical effect and mechanism
SSRIs and SNRIsDelayed orgasm or anorgasmia, lower desire (serotonergic). Bupropion and mirtazapine carry much less risk.
Dopamine-blocking antipsychotics (for example, risperidone)Raised prolactin suppresses GnRH, so desire falls; gynecomastia, galactorrhea, amenorrhea
Alpha-1 blockers and some antipsychoticsEjaculatory problems; rarely priapism
Spironolactone, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitorsAnti-androgen effects: lower desire, gynecomastia
Opioids, chronic alcoholLow testosterone and reduced desire

Paraphilias and paraphilic disorders

A paraphilia is an intense, persistent sexual interest outside the usual range. It becomes a paraphilic disorder only when, for at least 6 months, it causes the person distress or impairment, or the person has acted on it with someone who did not or could not consent. A consensual, non-distressing atypical interest is not a mental disorder.

DisorderFocus of arousal
VoyeuristicWatching an unsuspecting person undress or have sex
ExhibitionisticExposing the genitals to an unsuspecting person
FrotteuristicTouching or rubbing against a non-consenting person
Sexual masochism / sadismBeing humiliated or made to suffer / causing suffering
PedophilicPrepubescent children (the person is at least 16 and at least 5 years older)
FetishisticNon-living objects or non-genital body parts
TransvesticCross-dressing
High-yield: cross-dressing for arousal in a man who identifies as a man is not gender dysphoria; it is a transvestic interest, and a disorder only with distress or impairment.

s23e-s13a04.bodyHtml:
Terms

  • Sex assigned at birth: usually recorded from external genitalia.
  • Gender identity: a person's inner sense of their own gender, which may or may not match the sex assigned at birth. Transgender people have a gender identity that differs from it; cisgender people have one that matches it; some people are nonbinary.
  • Gender expression: how a person presents gender outwardly.
  • Sexual orientation: whom a person is attracted to. It is separate from gender identity.

Gender dysphoria

A diagnosis describing clinically significant distress or impairment that arises from a marked incongruence between experienced gender and assigned gender, lasting at least 6 months. Being transgender or gender-nonconforming is not itself a disorder; the diagnosis rests on the distress. Transgender people have higher rates of depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts, which studies link largely to stigma, rejection and discrimination (minority stress), and family and social support is protective.

How gender-affirming hormones work

DrugMechanismExpected effectsKey risks to monitor
TestosteroneAndrogen receptor agonistDeeper voice (permanent), facial and body hair, cessation of menses, clitoral growth, more muscle massErythrocytosis (androgens raise erythropoietin and suppress hepcidin), acne, lipid changes. It is teratogenic and is not a contraceptive.
EstradiolEstrogen receptor agonist; also suppresses LH and so testosteroneBreast growth, softer skin, fat redistribution, less body hairVenous thromboembolism, lowest with transdermal estradiol. Ethinyl estradiol is avoided because it is the most thrombogenic.
SpironolactoneAndrogen receptor antagonist and mineralocorticoid antagonistBlocks androgen effectsHyperkalemia, especially with ACE inhibitors, ARBs or kidney disease
GnRH agonistsContinuous stimulation down-regulates pituitary GnRH receptors, so LH, FSH and sex steroids fallSuppress gonadal hormone productionBone mineral density
Exam trap: a GnRH agonist given continuously suppresses the gonads; given in pulses it stimulates them.
High-yield: after gender-affirming surgery, screen the organs the person has: the prostate stays after vaginoplasty, and a cervix stays unless it was removed.

s23e-s13a05.bodyHtml:
Every drug of abuse raises dopamine release from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens (the mesolimbic reward pathway), directly or indirectly. Repeated use shifts control from pleasure toward habit and craving, and chronic exposure causes adaptive changes that are unmasked as withdrawal when the drug stops. A substance use disorder is a problematic pattern of use with features of impaired control, social impairment, risky use and pharmacological criteria (tolerance, withdrawal), graded mild, moderate or severe by the number of criteria met.

DrugMain mechanismIntoxicationWithdrawal
AlcoholEnhances GABA-A; inhibits NMDADisinhibition, ataxia, slurred speech, nystagmusTremor, sweating, tachycardia, seizures, delirium tremens (can be fatal)
BenzodiazepinesRaise the frequency of GABA-A chloride channel openingSedation; respiratory depression mainly with alcohol or opioidsLike alcohol: anxiety, tremor, seizures (can be fatal)
BarbituratesRaise the duration of channel openingSedation, respiratory depressionLike alcohol; severe
OpioidsMu-receptor agonists (Gi): less cAMP, K+ efflux, less presynaptic Ca2+ entryMiosis, respiratory depression, constipation, euphoriaMydriasis, yawning, tearing, rhinorrhea, piloerection, diarrhea, cramps; distressing but rarely fatal in adults
CocaineBlocks reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine and serotoninMydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension, chest pain, agitation, psychosisLow mood, fatigue, hypersomnia, increased appetite
AmphetaminesRelease monoamines (reverse transport through VMAT and the plasma membrane transporters)Like cocaine; prolonged psychosis, bruxismLike cocaine
NicotineAgonist at nicotinic receptors (alpha-4 beta-2 in the reward pathway)Alertness, appetite suppressionIrritability, anxiety, craving, more appetite
CannabisCB1 agonist (Gi, presynaptic)Conjunctival injection, appetite, dry mouth, slowed time, anxiety or paranoiaIrritability, insomnia, low appetite
PCP, ketamineNMDA receptor antagonistsAgitation, violence, horizontal and vertical nystagmus, analgesia, hypertensionNot clinically prominent
LSD, psilocybinSerotonin 5-HT2A agonistsPerceptual distortion, synesthesia, anxietyNone significant
MDMASerotonin (and other monoamine) releaseEuphoria, empathy, hyperthermia, bruxism, hyponatremiaLow mood

Drugs used to treat dependence

  • Buprenorphine: high-affinity partial mu agonist. Its ceiling on respiratory depression makes it safer than full agonists. Given to someone with a full agonist on board, it displaces that drug and causes sudden (precipitated) withdrawal.
  • Methadone: long-acting full mu agonist, metabolised by CYP3A4 and other enzymes; it prolongs the QT interval.
  • Naltrexone: mu antagonist; reduces the reward from alcohol and blocks opioids.
  • Varenicline: partial agonist at alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic receptors. It eases craving and blunts the reward of smoking.
  • Bupropion: inhibits norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake; lowers the seizure threshold.
Exam trap: pinpoint pupils point to opioids. Dilated pupils with yawning, tearing and gooseflesh point to opioid withdrawal.

s23e-s13a06.bodyHtml:
Metabolism

Ethanol is oxidised to acetaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase (and by CYP2E1, which is induced by heavy drinking). Acetaldehyde is oxidised to acetate by aldehyde dehydrogenase. Both steps reduce NAD+ to NADH. A high NADH/NAD+ ratio:

  • blocks gluconeogenesis (pyruvate is driven to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate), so a fasting drinker becomes hypoglycemic;
  • favours lactate, so lactic acidosis follows, and lactate competes with urate excretion (gout flares);
  • favours glycerol-3-phosphate and blocks fatty acid oxidation, so fatty liver develops;
  • contributes to alcoholic ketoacidosis, in which beta-hydroxybutyrate predominates.

Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase. Acetaldehyde builds up after a drink and causes flushing, nausea, vomiting, headache and palpitations. Metronidazole and some cephalosporins can cause a similar reaction. Fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase and is used for methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning.

Thiamine

Thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, transketolase and branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase. Deficiency starves neurons of aerobic energy. Glucose given to a deficient patient pushes more pyruvate into a blocked pathway, so thiamine is given before or with glucose. Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, ataxia) damages the mammillary bodies and the tissue around the third ventricle and aqueduct. Korsakoff syndrome adds lasting anterograde amnesia with confabulation.

Withdrawal

Chronic alcohol down-regulates GABA-A responsiveness and up-regulates NMDA glutamate receptors. When drinking stops, the brain is left over-excited.

The syndromes overlap and are best read as a timeline from the last drink. Minor withdrawal is the earliest and most common. Seizures are usually single or few. Hallucinosis is distinguished by a clear sensorium and normal vital signs. Delirium tremens combines fluctuating confusion with autonomic hyperactivity (fever, tachycardia, hypertension, sweating) and can be fatal.

High-yield: GGT and an AST/ALT ratio above 2 support heavy drinking, and an MCV above the normal range is common.

s23e-s13b01.bodyHtml:
Bereavement

  • Ordinary grief: support, information and follow-up. Medication is not needed, and a sedative-hypnotic for weeks after a death is not a treatment for grief.
  • Major depressive episode after a loss: diagnose and treat it like any depression (psychotherapy, an antidepressant, or both). Bereavement does not exclude the diagnosis.
  • Prolonged grief disorder (12 months or more in adults): grief-focused psychotherapy designed for the disorder works best. Treat coexisting depression as well.

Assessing suicide risk

  1. Ask directly and in plain words about thoughts of death or suicide.
  2. If present: how often, any plan, intent, preparation, access to means (firearms, stored medicines), past attempts, substance use, and protective factors.
  3. Collect information from family or others where possible, and document the reasoning.
PictureUsual disposition
Thoughts of death without plan or intent, good supports, engaged in careOutpatient care with a written safety plan, lethal-means counselling, treatment of the underlying disorder and early follow-up
Plan or intent, recent attempt, psychosis, intoxication, or no safe settingEmergency psychiatric evaluation and inpatient admission
Imminent danger and the person refuses admissionInvoluntary emergency hold under local law

Lethal-means counselling: ask about guns and medicines at home, and advise removing firearms or storing them locked and unloaded, and locking up or disposing of medicines. Restricting access to lethal means reduces suicide deaths. A "no-suicide contract" has no protective value and is not a substitute for assessment.

Treatments that lower suicide risk

  • Lithium in mood disorders and clozapine in schizophrenia both reduce suicidal behaviour.
  • Dialectical behaviour therapy reduces repeated self-harm in people with emotion dysregulation, including borderline personality disorder.
  • Cognitive therapy focused on suicide prevention, and brief contact after discharge, also help.
Exam trap: a first antidepressant prescription does not make an outpatient with a plan safe; the danger is now. Admit first, then treat.

s23e-s13b02.bodyHtml:
Intimate partner violence

  • Screen women of reproductive age, and ask any patient with suggestive clues, in private. Interview the patient without the partner present, and use a professional interpreter rather than a relative.
  • Be direct and non-judgemental. Believe the patient and say that violence is not their fault.
  • Assess immediate danger: escalating violence, threats to kill, weapons, attempted strangulation, pregnancy, children at risk.
  • Offer a safety plan, advocacy services and a hotline, and document injuries carefully in the patient's words with diagrams or photographs.
  • A competent adult decides whether to leave or report. Reporting duties for adults vary by state (for example, some injuries from weapons); child abuse must always be reported.
  • Couples counselling is not recommended while abuse is ongoing, because it can increase danger.

Elder abuse

Suspected abuse or neglect of an older or dependent adult is reportable to adult protective services in nearly every state, and the clinician does not need proof or the patient's consent. Interview the patient alone, examine fully, and admit to hospital if the person is unsafe at home.

Delirium in hospital

  1. Look for the cause: infection, drugs (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids), urinary retention, constipation, pain, hypoxia, electrolyte and glucose disturbance, withdrawal.
  2. Use non-drug measures first: reorientation, family presence, glasses and hearing aids, a day-night routine, early mobilisation, and removing catheters and restraints.
  3. Reserve a low-dose antipsychotic for severe agitation that puts the patient or staff at risk. Avoid benzodiazepines except in alcohol or sedative withdrawal.

Depression that looks like dementia

Older adults with depression may complain of poor memory, answer "I don't know" and give little effort on testing. After checking for reversible causes, treat the depression and reassess cognition. Late-life depression can also be an early sign of a neurodegenerative disease, so follow these patients.

Motivational interviewing in the clinic

StageWhat helps
PrecontemplationAsk permission to share information; personalised feedback without pressure
ContemplationExplore pros and cons; reflect both sides of the ambivalence
PreparationAgree a concrete plan and a start date; offer medication where it helps
Action and maintenanceReinforce progress, plan for high-risk situations, treat a lapse as information

s23e-s13b03.bodyHtml:
Erectile dysfunction

  • Take a sexual, medical and medication history. Gradual onset with loss of morning erections suggests an organic cause; sudden, situational loss with preserved morning erections suggests a psychological one.
  • Erectile dysfunction often precedes coronary disease by years: check glucose or HbA1c, lipids and blood pressure, and address smoking. Measure morning testosterone if desire is low or there are signs of hypogonadism.
  • First-line treatment: lifestyle change and a PDE5 inhibitor.
  • PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated with any nitrate (and with riociguat). Alternatives: vacuum erection device, intracavernosal or intraurethral alprostadil, or a penile prosthesis.
  • Use caution with alpha-blockers (start at a low dose; risk of hypotension).

Antidepressant-related sexual dysfunction

Options: wait for tolerance if it is early, lower the dose, switch to a lower-risk drug (bupropion, mirtazapine), or add bupropion, which preserves a response that has taken months to achieve. A PDE5 inhibitor helps antidepressant-related erectile dysfunction. Never stop an SSRI abruptly.

Other sexual dysfunctions

DisorderKey featuresManagement
Premature (early) ejaculationEjaculation within about a minute of penetration on most occasions, for at least 6 months, with distressBehavioural techniques; daily or on-demand SSRI (off-label); topical anaesthetic
Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorderPain, fear of pain or pelvic floor tightening with attempted penetrationPelvic floor physical therapy, graded vaginal dilators, cognitive behavioural therapy
Female sexual interest/arousal disorderPersistently reduced interest or arousal with distressLook for causes: depression, relationship problems, drugs, hyperprolactinemia, menopause; sex therapy. Specific drugs are approved for premenopausal women in selected cases.
Delayed ejaculation, female orgasmic disorderOften drug-related (SSRIs)Adjust the drug; sex therapy

In postmenopausal women, painful intercourse from genitourinary syndrome of menopause responds to lubricants, moisturisers and low-dose vaginal estrogen.

Paraphilic disorders

Treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy with relapse prevention. An SSRI can reduce the intensity of urges. In people at high risk of harming others, anti-androgen treatment (a GnRH agonist or medroxyprogesterone) lowers testosterone and sexual drive.

s23e-s13b04.bodyHtml:
Respectful care

  • Ask for and use the patient's name and pronouns, and record them. Use the patient's own words for their body where possible.
  • Take an organ inventory: screening follows the organs the person has, not the gender listed in the record.
  • Screen for depression, anxiety, suicidal thoughts, substance use and violence, which are more common because of stigma and rejection. Family acceptance is strongly protective, particularly for young people.

Screening by organ

OrganApproach
Cervix (transgender men and nonbinary people assigned female at birth)Cervical cancer screening on the same schedule as for anyone with a cervix; testosterone can make cytology samples harder to read
BreastTransgender men who have not had chest surgery are screened like other people with breasts; some tissue remains after chest masculinisation. For transgender women on estrogen, screening advice varies and follows specialist guidance.
Prostate (transgender women)The prostate is retained after vaginoplasty; it is usually palpable through the anterior wall of the neovagina. Shared decision-making as for others of the same age; PSA is lower on estrogen.

Monitoring hormone therapy

  • Testosterone: hematocrit and testosterone level. If the hematocrit rises above 54%, reduce or hold the dose (or change the formulation) and look for other causes such as sleep apnea or smoking. Testosterone does not prevent pregnancy and is teratogenic, so anyone who can become pregnant and has sex that could cause pregnancy needs contraception; an IUD or progestin-only method works well.
  • Estradiol: estradiol level, and testosterone if an anti-androgen is used. Advise stopping smoking because of thrombosis risk; transdermal estradiol has the lowest risk. Do not use ethinyl estradiol.
  • Spironolactone: potassium and creatinine, especially with ACE inhibitors, ARBs or kidney disease. If hyperkalemia occurs, stop it; other anti-androgen options exist.
  • Discuss fertility preservation before starting hormones or having gonadal surgery.

Young people

Gender-diverse children are supported without pressure toward any outcome. Decisions about medical treatment for adolescents are made by specialist multidisciplinary teams, and the rules and recommendations differ between countries and states and continue to change.

Exam trap: amenorrhea on testosterone does not mean a person cannot become pregnant.

s23e-s13b05.bodyHtml:
Screening and brief intervention

Screen adults for unhealthy alcohol use with a validated tool such as AUDIT-C or a single question about heavy-drinking days. A positive screen leads to a brief, non-judgemental intervention (feedback, advice, a goal) and assessment for alcohol use disorder, with referral or treatment when the disorder is present (screening, brief intervention and referral to treatment).

Withdrawal

  • Give thiamine before or with glucose to anyone at risk; never delay treating hypoglycemia.
  • Measure severity with CIWA-Ar in patients who can communicate. Benzodiazepines are the treatment: symptom-triggered dosing uses less drug than fixed schedules.
  • Long-acting agents (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam) give a smoother course. Lorazepam (no active metabolites) is preferred in advanced liver disease and in many older adults.
  • Delirium tremens: intensive care, escalating intravenous benzodiazepines, fluids, electrolytes and thiamine; phenobarbital or propofol for refractory cases. Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and do not treat withdrawal.
  • Outpatient management is reasonable only for mild withdrawal without past seizures or delirium tremens, serious illness or an unsafe home.

Medicines that reduce drinking

DrugBest useAvoid when
Naltrexone (oral or monthly injection)First line; reduces heavy drinkingTaking or needing opioids; acute hepatitis or liver failure
AcamprosateFirst line; maintains abstinence; safe in liver diseaseSevere kidney impairment (creatinine clearance 30 mL/min or less)
DisulfiramHighly motivated patients with supervised dosingNot yet abstinent; heart disease; psychosis; cannot comply
Gabapentin, topiramateOff-label alternativesKidney disease (gabapentin dose); cognitive side effects (topiramate)

Combine medication with psychosocial support (counselling, mutual-help groups) and treat coexisting psychiatric disorders.

Exam trap: hallucinations in a fully oriented patient with normal vital signs on day 1 or 2 are alcoholic hallucinosis, not delirium tremens.

s23e-s13b06.bodyHtml:
Opioid overdose

Support breathing (bag-mask ventilation) and give naloxone, repeating it as needed: potent synthetic opioids such as fentanyl may need several doses, and naloxone can wear off before a long-acting opioid, so observe the patient. Prescribe naloxone to anyone at risk and to their family.

Xylazine, an alpha-2 agonist sedative, is now a common adulterant of illicit fentanyl. It causes sedation, bradycardia and hypotension that naloxone does not reverse, and severe chronic skin wounds. Naloxone is still given for the opioid component; the rest is supportive.

Medications for opioid use disorder

  • Medication reduces overdose death. Buprenorphine can be prescribed by any clinician with a standard DEA registration; the separate waiver was removed in 2023. Start it once the patient has objective withdrawal, or use a low-dose start, to avoid precipitated withdrawal; after fentanyl the wait is often longer.
  • Methadone for opioid use disorder is dispensed through opioid treatment programmes. Watch the QT interval and interactions: CYP3A4 inducers such as rifampin lower its level and cause withdrawal.
  • Extended-release naltrexone needs about 7 to 10 days without opioids first.
  • Pregnancy: continue or start buprenorphine or methadone. Withdrawal management (detoxification) carries a high risk of relapse and overdose. The newborn is monitored for neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome.

Sedative withdrawal

Long-term benzodiazepine users who stop suddenly (for example, on hospital admission) can have seizures. Restart a benzodiazepine and taper slowly over weeks to months.

Stimulants

Cocaine or methamphetamine toxicity with agitation, tachycardia, hypertension or chest pain is treated first with benzodiazepines, cooling and supportive care. Do not give a beta-blocker alone early in cocaine toxicity. Evaluate chest pain for acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection and stroke.

Cannabis

Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome: years of heavy use, recurrent bouts of vomiting and abdominal pain, relief from hot showers. Acute care: fluids, haloperidol or topical capsaicin. The only lasting treatment is stopping cannabis.

Tobacco

  • Ask every patient about tobacco, advise quitting, and offer counselling and medication.
  • Varenicline or combination nicotine replacement (patch plus a short-acting form) are the most effective options. A large trial found no significant excess of neuropsychiatric events with varenicline or bupropion.
  • Bupropion is contraindicated with seizure disorders, bulimia or anorexia nervosa, and abrupt alcohol or sedative withdrawal.
Exam trap: a patient who still needs regular opioids for pain cannot take naltrexone for alcohol use disorder; choose acamprosate.
